speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext:
In accordance with the regular practice I wish to announce the appointment of the deputy postmaster general, effective
June 20. Mr. William Hugh Wilson is to fill the vacancy resulting from the forthcoming retirement of Mr. George A. Boyle, who has served for 45 years.
I should like to express appreciation on behalf of the government for the service Mr. Boyle has rendered. He has made many outstanding contributions to the development of Canada's postal service, particularly in the field of international postal affairs where he has represented Canada as vice-president of the executive and liaison committee of the universal postal union.
Mr. Wilson has been director of operations in the head office of the department since April, 1959. He entered the post office in 1929 as a temporary postal helper in Vancouver. He became postmaster in Vancouver in 1955, and in 1958 was named regional director of postal service for the Pacific region.
Mr. Wilson brings to the position of deputy postmaster general outstanding administrative skill and unusual ability to achieve results while maintaining the support of those who work for him. He has been responsible for numerous major innovations in postal techniques. As director of operations he has been responsible for all the aspects of the day to day operation of the postal service except matters of transportation.

subtopic: MISSION TO DISCUSS ENTRY BY U.K.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MISSION TO DISCUSS ENTRY BY U.K.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask him whether he has anything to report in regard to the success he has had in organizing a meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers to discuss Britain's entry into the common market.
Righf Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, if the house will allow me I should like to add to the remarks I made on June 9, 1961. At that time I stated that the government was convinced of the necessity for a proper balance being observed as between bilateral and collective consultation on this matter. I said at that time that I envisaged bilateral consultation both at the official and the ministerial levels, but that because of the potential consequences of United Kingdom membership in the common market I believed that the fullest consideration should be given to collective ministerial discussion and also, if necessary, to a meeting of prime ministers.
In the light of that statement there have been further exchanges with the United Kingdom government. As a result, arrangements are now being made for bilateral talks on a ministerial level to take place in Ottawa at a time to be arranged, probably in the second week of July, between the secretary of state for commonwealth relations, Right Hon. Duncan Sandys, and the Canadian ministers concerned-the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I also hope on that occasion to see Mr. Sandys.
[Mr. Herridge.l
In agreeing to these arrangements it has been made clear that the Canadian government will regard talks with Mr. Sandys as exploratory in nature and as not constituting the basis for any binding decision or understanding as to Canada's attitude in this matter. I say this because, while I acknowledge the value of preparatory exploration of the issues between the United Kingdom and Canadian governments, I am equally convinced of the necessity for these matters to be discussed by representatives of the commonwealth association meeting together.
Collective discussions were held in London some three weeks ago among senior officials of commonwealth countries, and I should hope that following the conversations which Mr. Sandys will have here, and other United Kingdom ministers in other countries of the commonwealth, it will then be thought appropriate and advisable for collective ministerial discussions to take place. There will be occasion for this in the regular way when the economic ministers of the commonwealth assemble for their fall meeting.
There has been comment in the United Kingdom and Canadian press about my reference last Friday to the need for a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in respect of this general subject. Some newspapers and commentators have assumed that what I called for was an immediate meeting of prime ministers. The reading of what I stated makes clear otherwise. I did not call for an immediate meeting of prime ministers; and also, in speaking of such a meeting, I said it should be held if necessary. What I wished to convey at that time, and I reiterate it now, is that I can envisage circumstances in which a meeting of prime ministers would be desirable and indeed necessary. It is not possible at this time to decide with certainty whether or not a meeting at prime ministerial level should take place. This is a matter which can only be decided in the light of developments and, in particular, on the outcome of the various bilateral and collective discussions and consultations which will take place.
I want once more, in answer to the question put by the hon. member, which is indicative of his interest in this matter, to emphasize the great importance to Canada, and indeed to the commonwealth association as a whole, of the United Kingdom's future relationship with the European economic community. The political and economic implications are so vast and complex that they deserve the most searching examination on the part of all countries concerned. It is this consideration, and of course in particular a concern for Canadian political and economic interests, which underlies the government's insistence on thorough and effective consultation.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON EXCHANGE OF LEAD FOR SURPLUS U.S. GRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: STATEMENT ON EXCHANGE OF LEAD FOR SURPLUS U.S. GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, June 9, I undertook to take as notice the question raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia as to whether the reported transaction between the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada and the United States authorities, involving the barter of Canadian lead for United States grain, would have any effect on Canada's own grain marketing policy.
I have now been informed that this transaction has been concluded and that it does not depart from the pattern of previous barter transactions entered into by the United States authorities in obtaining primary or strategic commodities under public law 480. From the government's standpoint this is a private business transaction concluded by a private Canadian firm and, as the hon. member is aware, the government does not interfere in private business transactions. Our only concern is that the sale of surplus grain thus acquired through barter will not displace normal commercial sales of grain. On this point we have been assured that this barter transaction will be subject to the same safeguards as those already established and agreed upon, and which have been applied in the past for the protection of our commercial marketing areas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 10 the hon. member for Assiniboia asked for my comments in connection with a recent incident in Toronto in which children were in contact with some powder containing radium, which they discovered in a warehouse.
I should like to pay tribute to the prompt and efficient manner in which the local authorities acted, which seems to have averted the danger of any serious results. On the basis of all the information received there seems to be no reason to expect that any of the persons involved will suffer any ill effects. The last stages of the clean-up and accounting process are now going on under the immediate direction of officers of the Ontario department of health.
During world war II large amounts of radium powder were used to paint luminous dials in aircraft and other equipment. It seems clear that the supplies in this case came from that source and were obtained before 1947, when the regulations of the atomic energy control board came into effect. Such material cannot now be acquired except under licence from the board, and licences are not granted unless the board is satisfied, on the advice of its health advisers, that the recipient has adequate knowledge and facilities to ensure that no health hazard will result.
It may be that some of the radium powder obtained prior to 1947 is still stored in industrial establishments, warehouses and similar places. After so many years the material will have lost its usefulness for the painting of luminous dials, but it will remain a potential danger to health because of its radioactivity. I wish, therefore, to advise all organizations to make quite sure that they do not have in storage any old stocks of radium luminous compound. My colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, whose department advises the atomic energy control board on matters relating to health and safety, suggests that the radiation protection division of his department be notified if any such material is found. That division

can then make arrangements for proper disposal, which should not be attempted by other parties.
Meanwhile, every effort is being made to locate any other supplies that may still be in existence under similar circumstances.

I should like now to give the reasons that would have prompted me to take exception, not to the bill itself, but to section 15 in particular.

Mr. Speaker, in 1959, following representations made by various pilots' associations and several members of parliament, the then minister of transport withdrew Bill S-3 to exempt any ship designated by the governor in council from the obligation of paying pilotage dues.
The government undoubtedly realized that their action was too drastic and they decided to proceed by steps but, I repeat, always with a view to abolishing pilotage all along the St. Lawrence.
That, in my opinion, is why section 15 was inserted in the bill we now have before us.
Indeed, section 15 stipulates that American lakers will be exempt from the obligation of paying pilotage dues in the St. Regis district down to Montreal, that is in an exclusively Canadian zone.
The scheme is clever. The exemption is only for that section for the time being but, in a few years from now, it will be extended to the whole length of the river.
Canada Shipping Act
The minister may tell us, as he did before the committee, that it will not be so. I am quite willing to take his word for it but, on the other hand, he will agree with me that his statement binds neither his successor nor the government.
The assurance he has given to the committee is no guarantee for the pilots as far as the future is concerned.
When this bill was examined in committee, we had the opportunity of hearing the legal adviser of the St. Lawrence pilots' federation and the representative of the Canadian merchant service guild.
These two representatives indicated before the committee that they took particular exception to clause 15 first on grounds of national sovereignty and then on grounds of safety in navigation.
The matter of sovereignty and of treaties was clearly dealt with yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I will not therefore take it up again.
As for the question of safety, it must first be recognized that with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, the traffic is bound to increase considerably in the coming years. Moreover, as the ships plying those waters will be bigger and speedier, the danger will be greater. The logical thing to do then, Mr. Speaker, is to render more stringent the safety measures, not to relax them. As a matter of fact, that is what we have been doing for several years now in the case of highways. In order to insure the greatest safety on our highways, the traffic laws have been tightened each year.
When asked by the members of the committee to comment upon the conditions of navigation in the district concerned, Mr. Guy Chartier, president of the Cornwall district pilot association, stated that the channel was quite narrow and difficult. He added that in his opinion no one should be allowed to pilot a ship in those waters unless he had been plying them for six or seven years. He also remarked that on the Canadian side, before getting a pilot licence, one had to have a master licence and two years of navigation in this area after apprenticeship while, on the American side, licence is granted after 12 trips only, which gave him reason to conclude unhesitatingly that such persons could not be qualified to navigate in that district.

Would my hon. friend allow me a question?

Surely.
Is he not aware that it is absolutely forbidden to any American pilot to pilot a ship in Canadian waters, between St. Regis and Montreal?

I wish to point out, that it is strange that the Department of Transport does not require the American masters-and I repeat the point the minister and I just mentioned-to pass tests before they are permitted to pilot their ships in exclusively Canadian waters. It seems to me that we should expect from the American masters the same qualifications and the same degree of experience as we expect from our own pilots.
Therefore, it seems clear to me according to the views of experienced men, that to exempt those ships of the payment of pilotage dues would endanger the safety of navigation in that area. Furthermore, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, the adoption of clause 15 would be a step toward the abolition of compulsory pilotage by Canadian pilots in the other districts of the St. Lawrence river.
The minister is aware that strong representations have been made in Washington- and there is no call to doubt their continuance in the future-to grant the American lakers the same privileges upon the whole length of the St. Lawrence river.

Mr. Speaker, it was suggested during the committee stage of this bill that Canada had given up something but had not received in return a quid pro quo. I should like to deal with that point for just a moment or two.
I should like to refer to pages 1 and 2 of the treaty between Canada and the United States dated May 5, 1961. At page 1 it is provided that the President of the United States by proclamation may declare certain areas compulsory pilotage areas, and listed there are districts Nos. 1, 2 and 3. Without reading the detailed descriptions, district No. 1 is the St. Lawrence area between St. Regis and Kingston, district No. 2 is roughly the area of the St. Clair river, and, district No. 3 is the area of the St. Mary's river and Sault Ste. Marie.
I should like to read the paragraph following the description of those districts, which is as follows:
Registered vessels of the United States and foreign vessels navigating United States waters of the great lakes which are not designated by the president by proclamation-
That refers to the three preceding areas that have been designated. I continue:
-are required by the act to have on board a United States registered pilot or a Canadian registered pilot or other officer qualified for the waters concerned

To me, and I think to anyone who reads it, that is a clear indication that Canada does receive some rights in United States waters and the great lakes, particularly the waters of lake Michigan.
There was a question asked in the committee as to why this matter of having a pilot or not having a pilot betweeen St. Regis and Montreal was not covered by the treaty. One answer is that the waters are exclusively Canadian. I think perhaps an analogy can be made regarding the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. In order to make a workable navigation seaway in Canada, certain work had to be done on the canals between St. Regis and Montreal. That work was done at a cost to and by the Canadian government because it is exclusively Canadian waters. Would the United States government have spent the $100 million odd it did spend without having the assurance from the Canadian government that it was going to improve the channel between St. Regis and Montreal?

I think the analogy is clear there. The United States government would not have given us a general pilotage agreement concerning the whole of the St. Lawrence system without having received an undertaking or understanding that certain provisions would be made for it in respect to that section of the St. Lawrence seaway from St. Regis to Montreal.
I am not sure that the argument of the hon. member for Levis is valid when he says this is only a first step. I cannot go as far as he does, because it seems to me quite clear that Montreal is the end of the seaway works built either by Canada or the United States, and there would be no validity in a United States request for pilotage rights beyond Montreal by reason of that fact. It is true, of course, that the traffic between the United States and Canada, in that section from Seven Islands to the Ohio steel ports on the United States side, is increasing and that possibly fewer ships than heretofore will now turn around at Montreal, although I think for some years Montreal will be essentially the eastern terminal of the seaway in regard to grain shipments.
Again I should like to emphasize the fact that there has not been any clear indication as to the matter of safety. Sometimes we tend to make open assumptions that when an accident happened at a time when there was no pilot on board, it happened because there was no pilot on board. I do not think our pilots would be happy if we made the similar assumption that because there was a pilot on board at the time an accident happened, it was his fault. As I pointed out in committee, I hope better statistics and records are kept so that more detailed statistics can be published. If this is done we will then have the opportunity of assessing that portion of responsibility for an accident which is attributable to the fact that a pilot was not on board.

First of all, for the hon. member's information, I should tell him that the Department of Transport gives the St. Lawrence pilots a remarkably good treatment. In fact,
I think there are few Canadian corporations whose employees are so highly paid proportionately to their work. I realize that pilots have responsibilities, and my department has always seen to it that their salaries or dues be guaranteed and in line with their responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing we seem to forget sometimes about our pilots: our primary concern should be the safety of navigation on the St. Lawrence river. On the other hand, if we impose all sorts of charges and give rise to all sorts of difficulties, if, in a word, we enforce special procedures for vessels using the St. Lawrence river, there is a risk of less efficiency in the St. Lawrence shipping trade.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in our discussion with the United States, in order to come to some agreement with regard to piloting on the great lakes or any other waterway where both countries have a common interest, we must keep in mind that the safety of navigation must be the prime consideration. The same applies to the efficiency of seaway traffic. We do not wish ships to be hampered in their business; on the contrary, they should be able to go about their business in a logical way. That is why, in those discussions with the United States, we always have in mind not only the improvement of seaway traffic but also the protection of the Canadian pilots' position, their salaries and the part they play in the seaway traffic of this country.
That is why in this case, when we had to negotiate with the United States, we came to an agreement which, to my mind, is justified. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) explained a

Canada Shipping Act
moment ago, the Americans also made some concessions, and I am convinced that the agreement which has been concluded is entirely reasonable, as not a single Canadian pilot will lose a cent because American vessels benefit from an exemption. Not a single Canadian pilot will lose his job following this arrangement, because we did insist that no American pilot be entitled to do any piloting on the St. Lawrence river, between St. Regis and Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Levis suggested a moment ago that the Department of Transport did not seem to care too much about the fate of our Canadian pilots, and that our officials seemed to want to please the Americans. Well, I must point out to him that the Department of Transport guarantees very attractive salaries to the pilots, and that there are not many Canadian corporations which pay their staff a salary of about $12,000 a year, not including an expense allowance of up to a couple of thousand dollars, and all that for eight or nine months of work.
I know Canadian pilots have responsibilities and that their services are most important to shipping and in many other ways. Just the same, they are paid very attractive salaries. Members of the Canadian corporation of pilots enjoy rights based on an ancient tradition which I respect as much as anyone else; however, in view of the fact that the Department of Transport guarantees jobs and fees to Canadian pilots, I feel they enjoy great benefits under our legislation.
Would the minister allow me a question? What will happen to the pilots in the Cornwall-Montreal area?
I beg your pardon?
What will happen to the pilots in the Cornwall-Montreal district if, within a few years, all American ships can be piloted by Americans?

I am very pleased that my hon. friend has asked this question because as Minister of Transport, I was asked by the pilots themselves to grant compulsory pilotage in that district. In fact, in November 1960,
I told them: Your request is a serious one, and we shall do our utmost to grant it. After studying the matter, we imposed compulsory pilotage on all foreign ships. At the time, I indicated to the pilots that I was not prepared to impose compulsory pilotage on

American ships because we were then discussing pilotage on the great lakes. However, I asked the pilots to grant voluntary exemptions to American ships until the Canada Shipping Act was amended. Well, that is what happened, and the pilots themselves exempted American ships.
My hon. friend has asked what will happen to the pilots in that district. Well, their position is better today than it was in November 1960. We have improved their position. Moreover, I would point out to those who feel inclined to raise cries of persecution in a case like this, that I think there is a tendency to make a bogey out of everything that is done by the Department of Transport in regard to pilotage.
These pilots are members of an old association with traditions going back many years. They are jealous of their rights, and you may be sure I respect those rights. However, representations are constantly being made as if we wanted to deprive them of their livelihood. There is always a hue and cry whenever a word is changed in any document dealing with pilotage.
Pilots are now organized in a federation, they have well defined districts, their working hours have been reduced, their salaries and expense allowances have gone up from year to year. Considering that they were granted compulsory pilotage on all foreign vessels under the sole condition that American vessels be exempted, I feel that the pilots should not raise any bogey in such a case, because their situation has improved in that district since last November. It should be kept in mind especially that those districts did not even exist before. There was only the Ottawa-St. Lawrence district where pilotage was not compulsory. Consequently, they were at a disadvantage as compared with the pilots downstream from Montreal. Their position is much better nowadays. Pilotage has become compulsory. Their association is recognized and so are their districts. I think they have made a great step forward.
I know they did not get everything they wanted, but they have made a great step forward.
I feel that our agreement with the United States concerning the great lakes is both reasonable and justifiable. We did not twist their arm. We ensured fair treatment for our pilots. The United States agreed to our request, namely that there should be equal treatment right from the first year. They made

that concession and, in return, we made concessions on other points.
Consequently, I feel that as far as pilotage on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence is concerned, the pilots' situation is better now than it has ever been.

Now, after having agreed to that in November, exemption is intended for American ships. Well, pilots are objecting to that.
There is no question of raising cries of persecution or of making a bogey out of that. Neither the hon. member for Levis, nor I ever said any such thing. The minister says they are well treated and that their remuneration is excellent. Remuneration or salaries are not involved in that legislation; only two things are involved: upholding of sovereignty and protection against accidents.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND RECOMMEND CHANGES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND RECOMMEND CHANGES
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to consider and recommend changes that may be desirable in the War Measures Act;
That the committee consist of fifteen members to be designated by the house;
That the committee be empowered to sit during the sittings of the house;
That the committee have power to send for persons and papers;
That the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as it may deem advisable and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation to the printing thereof; and
That the committee be empowered to report from time to time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, ever since 1914 there has been on the statute books of this country an act known as the War Measures Act, which

was passed immediately after the commencement of the first great war. Following that war there were discussions on various occasions both in the House of Commons and in the other place regarding this legislation, particularly as to whether or not it should continue in effect following the declaration of peace.
The act in question, and I shall make only a short reference to it, provides for the issue of a proclamation by Her Majesty, or under the authority of the governor in council, who may then "do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada"; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms-"the power to censor, control and suppress publications, writings, communications and means of communications, arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation, control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters, and the movement of vessels in Canada, and also the control of transportation by land, air or water, control of trade, exportation, importation, production and manufacture, as well as appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property". In other words, under the general powers there is virtually nothing that the governor in council cannot do within the powers granted by the act.
Following the second world war the government of Right Hon. Mackenzie King and later the government of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent brought in and had passed by parliament two acts which contained virtually the same powers as the War Measures Act, and enabled the governor in council to draft orders in council which, regardless of whether or not they were infringements on provincial jurisdiction, were none the less lawful.
In 1960 parliament passed the bill of rights and made certain provisions therein respecting some of the powers contained in the War Measures Act. Section 6 of the War Measures Act reads as follows:
The provisions of the three sections last preceding shall only be in force during war. invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended.
Those are the sections giving the power, imposing penalties, and providing that anyone held for deportation under this act, or under arrest and detention as an alien enemy, or upon suspicion of being an alien enemy, or to prevent his departure from Canada, shall be released upon bail or otherwise discharged or tried, without the consent of the Minister of Justice.

The bill of rights provides that section 6 of the War Measures Act is repealed and substitutes therefor the following:
Sections 3, 4 and 5 shall come into force only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists.
For the protection of the rights of parliament there is this provision. The proclamation declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue or, if parliament is not then sitting, within the first 15 days next thereafter. A further subsection provides that when the proclamation has been laid before parliament a notice of motion in either house signed by 10 members thereof, praying that the proclamation be revoked, shall be debated in that house at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the motion in the house is made. This section further provides that if both houses of parliament resolve that the proclamation be revoked, it shall cease to have effect. In other words there was restored to parliament the right to assure that the executive power exercised by the governor in council shall be subject to the elected representatives of the people.
Various hon. gentlemen participated in the debate on the bill of rights. I am not going to refer to what they said, but I would point out that their views are dealt with at length in Hansard of August 3, 1960, at page 7503, when clause 6 of the War Measures Act, as part of the bill of rights, was before the house. Various suggestions were made for amendments to the War Measures Act. At that time I said, as reported at page 7506:
If a committee is set up and, of course, I am in the hands of the house as always-
To which the hon. member for Essex East with his customary suavity remarked as follows:
The right hon. gentleman has some influence.
I said:
I thank my hon. friend for those kind words. His geniality has brought about the recognition of a fact that he often denies.
This would be a most important contribution to the Canada of today and to the Canada of the future. At that time we would not deal as we are asked to now on a piecemeal basis with the rights under the War Measures Act. If there is a degree of unanimity, and I think there will be, that Canadian citizens should not be deported the committee might make that recommendation along with such other recommendations as will bring about a war measures act which on the one hand will maintain the solidarity and security of the state and on the other hand will have before it the paramount necessity of not needlessly sacrificing the rights of Canadians.
Committee on War Measures Act
That summarizes the general tenor of the views expressed by me and also by the Minister of Justice. Later at page 7511 of Hansard I said:
In so far as this is concerned-
I was referring to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition.
-no naturalized Canadian may be deprived of his citizenship and no naturalized British subject may be deprived of his status as a British subject under this act, and we accept that as a desirable objective when full and complete amendment of the War Measures Act or other acts is made.
There seemed to be general agreement at that time that there was the necessity for parliament to have the opportunity to deal with this matter. It is not a partisan matter. I am not going into anything which by the greatest exaggeration could be considered as bringing partisan considerations into this debate. I simply say there was agreement that something should be done to bring about amendments to the War Measures Act and to assure that the act, while maintaining the need of security at all times, should be so altered or changed as to provide that security, while at the same time preserving to the greatest degree possible the rights of the individual.
On January 27, 1961, at page 1475 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition asked me this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he could confirm or deny a report in the press this morning to the effect that during this session the government is going to amend the War Measures Act?
I replied:
I did not see that report. The government feels -and it expressed its feeling in this regard at the time discussions were taking place relative to the bill of rights-that some committee of the house might well consider the War Measures Act and, having considered it, make recommendations as to what revisions or amendments could be made to that act to render it a measure from which injustice would not follow.
A little later on I said:
I feel and I think the Leader of the Opposition will agree, that a full and complete review of the War Measures Act would be following a course in keeping with the desires of Canadians as a whole. In time of war the measure is necessary in the interests of maintaining security, but in the days of peace there cannot be too large a degree of justification for its maintenance in effect without giving parliament at least the opportunity, through a committee, of fully considering the representations that have been made from time to time with regard to this legislation.
Following that, the hon. member for Essex East indicated that a private member had a bill on the order paper showing the intention to introduce amendments to the War Measures Act. With customary modesty he did not refer to himself but simply said an hon. member had such a bill on the order paper. Later, on

Committee on War Measures Act May 29, the Leader of the Opposition asked this question as recorded at page 5504 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister, having regard to the statements made by him during the debate last year on the bill of rights and similar statements on January 27 this year, whether the government intends to submit the War Measures Act to this session of parliament for consideration?
To which I replied:
I can only say at this time that depending on the progress that is made in the house, a decision in that regard will be announced to the house.
Again a supplementary question was asked by the hon. member for Essex East. All this indicates, I think, that there is a desire to bring about a close scrutiny and examination of this legislation. I had hoped to bring it before the house yesterday, but in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition and at the request of the hon. member for Laurier the motion was set over until today.

speechtext:
I hope the house will accept this motion. I realize that many hon. members will argue, as they have argued throughout the session, that committees are becoming too numerous. This committee is one on which I am sure all who are chosen will be most happy and honoured to serve. It is the kind of constructive work in which members who wish to devote themselves to the maintenance of our freedoms will naturally desire to take part.
The question might arise as to how long this committee would sit. I think a start should be made. Many representations were made in 1960 and prior thereto. Various groups of lawyers, constitutional law professors and professors of history made representations. Professor Lower, professor emeritus of Queen's, has given many years of study to this question. I think of others equally well in-tentioned and well equipped who would be most desirous of playing their parts in this investigation and examination, and also in making recommendations consonant with the purpose of the legislation, but at the same time assuring the preservation of those things that should not be denied to Canadians.
This is now the 13th of June. I have no idea how long the session will continue, but the progress that has been made would seem to lend support to the hope that by the end of this month we should be in a position to conclude. If, however, we are not, I want the house to make its own determination. In that regard I return to a view that I expressed earlier, that in the interests of hon. members, particularly those with families including


small children, they should not be denied the opportunity to be with their families during the months of July and August.
During the summer the committee might conceivably exchange ideas and views on this particular matter and have representations made while not necessarily having to convene. In that way the committee would perform its duty without inconvenience or interfering with the legitimate desires of members not only to do that to which I have already referred, but also to see their constituents. Therefore, without further argument, I place this motion before the house. It may be contended it should have been done earlier. That will always be an argument; but if it had been done there would have been one more committee in addition to the number already sitting, about which complaint has been made.
Is this a necessary work to be done? I think it is. I do not feel that recommendations for amendment of this legislation should be the prerogative of departmental officials or cabinet ministers. This legislation crosses all party lines, and members of the committee when chosen will be able to do something to meet the anomalous situation which has prevailed in two world wars and following, that while we fought for freedom we found it necessary to place in bond as security for their preservation, the freedoms for which we fought.
I hope the house will accept this motion so the committee may commence the discharge of its duties and make decisions as to such suggestion as I made earlier, so as to enable not only the exchange of ideas between members of the committee, but also the reception of ideas from those learned in the law and also those learned in the processes of freedom. Then, the committee may bring about recommendations which will maintain the essence of the War Measures Act as the instrument for the mobilization of our people should war ever come and at the same time preserve so far as possible those things which are dearer than life itself.

And to the extent indicated in the bill of rights itself, to which I will make reference in a moment. The Prime Minister has suggested that because of the importance of this measure and the common attitude that prevails about considering amendments, this is not in itself the kind of question that should divide the house. I readily agree that such is the case. The Prime Minister will not expect me, of course, to refrain from putting on the record with regard to this matter which seem desirable in the light of the position we took last session with regard to amendments to the War Measures Act. However, with his general statement I do not quarrel.
The Prime Minister will recall, as he himself has reminded us by his several references to Hansard, that questions were put to the government and in particular to the Prime Minister asking when steps would be taken to bring about amendments to the War Measures Act. The Prime Minister mentioned one of the replies he made in which he said by way of response, I think somewhat vaguely, that it would depend largely on the progress that was made during the course of the present session.
I take the position, of course, that this is not the view the Prime Minister took when we discussed this matter in 1960. I believe his words in that regard, to which I will refer later, were more definitive than was the indication given in reply to the questions put to him during the course of this session by the Leader of the Opposition.
The Prime Minister has referred to the fact that there is now on the order paper a bill standing in my name which embodies the proposed amendments to the War Measures Act which were submitted last session in this house by the Leader of the Opposition and later in the committee on the bill of rights, by me, supported by the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve-Rosemont.
The practical consideration, however, is one that we must bear in mind. The government brings in, on the 13th day of June, a proposal that a committee should be established for the purpose of considering the War Measures Act and any amendments thereto. Under our procedures a bill introduced by the

Committee on War Measures Act government, of course, will likely have precedence over a bill proposed by a private member of this house. If it is a fact that my bill, which obviously encouraged the government at long last to take some action, is to be superseded by the action taken today by the government, then of course I can have no legitimate procedural complaint, nor would any such complaint get very far. I would be practical enough to recognize that situation at once.
That being the case, and if this is the government's final stand in the matter, as one who wants to see amendments to the War Measures Act and who wants to see the War Measures Act brought into a position consistent with the bill of rights I would under those conditions, of course, support the motion proposed today by the Prime Minister. However, I would do that not without some complaint on other grounds.
It is regrettable that this particular motion was not presented early in the session. We have complained from time to time that the government's mismanagement of the business of this house has been such as to crowd in, in the dying days of the session, not only much important legislation to be considered exclusively in this chamber, and other legislation to be considered by parliamentary committees, but as well the work of many of the standing and special committees of this house, with the result that not only are we sitting from 11 o'clock in the morning until 10.30 o'clock at night in the House of Commons but at the same time we have obligations in committees that are meeting simultaneously, some three times, some four times and on one occasion five times in a day, with one committee actually having had its sittings-I refer to the external affairs committee which is an extremely important one-during the luncheon recess from one o'clock until two thirty in the afternoon.
With the background of this heavy schedule for our committee and house work, the government now comes forward at this late moment to present this motion, which could well have been presented in the month of January. If it had been presented at that time, ample opportunity this session would have been provided for consultation with law experts and other competent people outside to assist in our deliberations of the amendments thought desirable in the War Measures Act.
The Prime Minister will therefore not be surprised if, seeking to be as conciliatory as possible at this time of the session, I lay before him with some justification our complaint for not having brought this measure forward early in the session. That was the time to bring forward something about which the government had been properly forewarned and

which indeed the Prime Minister himself, as he indicated in what he said today, had suggested to the house would be the action taken by the government during the course of the present session. I believe this matter is so important that we ought to begin the work of this committee at once, if that is to be the procedural situation in relation to the bill now standing in my name.
The Prime Minister has referred to some observations of Professor Lower. I am not surprised that he should do so, because Professor Lower obviously is a protagonist of the Prime Minister. He made that fact clear in the committee on the bill of rights when he spoke glowingly of the Prime Minister's efforts and generally of certain other points of view and positions taken by the Prime Minister.
I do not fail to recognize the merits of Professor Lower, although I would not be as enthusiastic, and the Prime Minister would not expect me to be-

I am going to quote him. I would not be as enthusiastic nor would the Prime Minister expect me to be as enthusiastic about him as within this limited context Professor Lower has been of the Prime Minister. However, Professor Lower made this statement, and I refer to page 5650 of Hansard of July 1, 1960, and to words quoted by the Leader of the Opposition:
I submit that if we are going to have a bill of rights in Canada, and there will be a great deal of debate about it, we ought to have one that means something. I believe that in normal peacetime our liberties are not in very serious danger. But in wartime they are in very serious danger, the liberties of all of us. Hence, it is the duty of the government to find a method of enacting legislation which will give at least minimum guarantees. Suggestions could be made which would modify the War Measures Act. In the meantime, as long as it is on the books it is the duty of everybody who loves a free society, who loves liberty, to bend his best efforts to attack this act and try to get rid of this invidious liberty-destroying statute, the War Measures Act.
I do not agree, and I am sure the Prime Minister does not agree, with this full denunciation of the War Measures Act, because I think we feel that human liberty already recognizes that in wartime there are certain exigencies in the interests of the security of the state which must be borne in mind. Professor Lower has expressed his views in a number of other publications. In the Canadian Commentator of March, 1959, he wrote an article entitled "The Bill of Rights" in which he said:
The Canadian War Measures Act is the most iniquitous piece of legislation ever to disgrace a British statute book-at least since the celebrated legislation-by-proclamations act of Henry VIII, 400 years ago. Its parallel is to be found not in any

other English-speaking country, for none have disgraced themselves in this respect as has Canada done-*
Then he went on to say:
If Mr. Diefenbaker, in the fullness of his wisdom, decided tomorrow that a state of apprehended insurrection existed, and proclaimed the War Measures Act, he could call parliament and the immense liberty-loving Conservative majority behind him, shocked at his conduct, might then proceed by open vote in the commons, to require him to withdraw his proclamation. Yes. So the Prime Minister is right in saying that Professor Lower had strong views about the War Measures Act, particularly in relation to the bill of rights. It is a fact that in the committee on the bill of rights I asked Professor Lower whether in view of his strongly expressed views regarding the War Measures Act he did not think appropriate amendments should be made to that act in the bill of rights. He answered in the affirmative. I think I should point out, in fairness, that after I left the room the Minister of Justice -and this is a matter of record in Hansard; the minister was not taking advantage of my absence and it was a mere coincidence; I mean that sincerely-put questions to Professor Lower and as a result got from him replies in direct contradiction to the position he had taken earlier in the committee.
This does not in any way affect the merits of the proposal now before the house, but since Professor Lower's name was mentioned I thought I should let the Prime Minister know that I was not unaware that this great admirer of his had strong views on this matter, views which in principle if not in every detail coincide with those expressed by the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke in this house on the occasion of the second reading of the bill of rights. On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition pointed out that the only change made in the bill of rights regarding the War Measures Act was to make possible parliamentary debate on the proclamation of the War Measures Act, which of course brings that act into force, and on its revocation. The bill of 90205-6-395J
13. 1961
Committee on War Measures Act rights provides that after such debate parliament may take a particular course of action as to whether or not it wishes to withdraw the proclamation. The point is that there was reference in the bill of rights to the War Measures Act, but only within the limited terms I have just mentioned.
The Leader of the Opposition urged that there should be amendments to the War Measures Act, and that these amendments should be incorporated in the bill of rights. While he recognized that the mere reference to the War Measures Act in section 5 of the bill of rights represented an improvement, he argued that it did not go far enough. The Leader of the Opposition said that because of the way the bill of rights dealt with the War Measures Act we were giving to the latter a greater sanctity and a greater prestige than was necessary or desirable, and that we were giving it as well a pre-eminence by that kind of amendment, rather than dealing with it in its form.
The Leader of the Opposition also pointed out that notwithstanding this provision in the bill of rights the law would remain in such a position that whatever had been done before would continue to be possible, notwithstanding the passage of the bill of rights. But he did point out-I think this is important for us to note, and it is something that Professor Lower has not taken into consideration-that we have to take into account war emergencies and, while that is the case, he would be a bold man who would argue that war emergencies may not make it necessary in the future for persons to be detained in a manner that apart from the exigencies of war would seem undesirable, not because of any act they had done but because of the danger of what they might do with regard to certain acts which obviously would involve the security of the state.
The War Measures Act, as the Prime Minister said, was placed on the statute books in 1914. As the Prime Minister said, it gives to the governor in council, in time of war, virtually unlimited powers to restrain the freedom of the person of the Canadian citizen. The Prime Minister did not note, however, that since the passage of the act we have adopted in our own Canadian Citizenship Act legislation that now makes it impossible for the government in peacetime to deprive any Canadian citizen, resident in Canada, of his citizenship.
Notwithstanding that, the Leader of the Opposition urged that we should now go a step forward. He said that any bill of rights should contain a provision limiting the powers given to the governor in council under the War Measures Act by expressly excluding from those powers the power by order in

Committee on War Measures Act council to deprive any Canadian citizen of his citizenship. The Leader of the Opposition argued, and I believe we would all agree with this, that the governor in council should be expressly forbidden to act under the War Measures Act to banish or exile any citizen from our country. I think we would wish it were possible to agree that the governor in council should be expressly forbidden, even in wartime, to detain any citizen or resident of our country without providing for an early trial on charges specifically laid in accordance with the law of Canada.
However, I am sure careful reflection will suggest that this would not be a responsible thing for parliament to do, and we are not prepared to go that far. Certainly in the bill I have before this house we do not take that extreme position. Nevertheless we in this party do feel that there should be, in the light of all that has transpired, a limitation by law on the absolute and arbitrary power of the governor in council to detain persons, even in wartime. We believe that a provision should have been written into the bill of rights which would limit the power of the governor in council to detain any person for more than let us say three months, or the period might be less, without a hearing before a supreme court judge and satisfying that judge that there were serious grounds for believing that the detention of such person was essential to the security of the state.
This measure, in so far as the Prime Minister is concerned, admittedly has a long association. I remind the Prime Minister that it was on May 16, 1947, when he as a private member of this house recommended not only that there should be amendments to the War Measures Act but as well that the Official Secrets Act should be repealed. The latter act was objectionable, I suppose, on the ground that it presumed guilt on the part of an accused contrary to the common law tradition which has existed for a long time and contrary to section 3(f) of the bill of rights, which now guarantees by law that an accused person is presumed to be innocent until proven otherwise.
The Prime Minister said in 1960 when this matter was discussed, as may be found on page 5948 of Hansard for July 7 of that year:
I think the whole act-
He was referring, of course, to the War Measures Act.
-deserves to be considered... I think if we could get together the membership in the house and deal with the War Measures Act and ascertain the degree to which the rights of the individual may be maintained to the highest extent without detriment to the security of the nation as a whole, changes and amendments might be made to that act. If hon. members of the house so desire, I would be willing that at the next session a committee

be set up to consider this whole field, for the War Measures Act, like all measures passed for the purpose of ensuring the salvation and survival of the state, has been found in the light of experience not only here but in other countries to contain provisions that ought to be ameliorated or subdued in the interests of the individual while at the same time maintaining the security of the state.
The Prime Minister referred to some parts of this discussion, but I did not note that he read all that was relevant. I may be wrong in that particular. I formed the impression, listening to the recital of what he did say in 1960, that he did not give the full text as I find it before me now in volume 6 of Hansard for last session. I had been urging, as indeed, had the Leader of the Opposition, that we should incorporate into the bill of rights certain amendments which we proposed. By such incorporation, we would bring the War Measures Act, without depriving it of its desired strength, into a form consistent with the bill of rights.

In any event, in the dying days of the session we are now faced with a proposal that might well have been brought forward by the government at the beginning of the session, particularly in the face of the assurance given by the Prime Minister last session. In my judgment, to have waited all this time demonstrates that the government was not as concerned about those amendments as it professes to be. It would not have been difficult for the government to come forward with this proposal early in the session when we could have given the matter the fullest consideration. However, it has chosen another course. It has chosen to increase our work in the dying days of the session in such a manner as to make it impossible for every member to give full consideration to the work of the house. There is not a member within sound of my voice who does not know that what I am saying is true. That is the situation. The country knows it. The country must know the kind of pressure that has been put upon us in the dying days of the session in the effort to discharge our duties.
However, the government has finally brought forward this measure. I hope the committee will be set up forthwith. I hope an opportunity will be given us to call the necessary persons to consider whether amendments should be made to the War Measures Act consistent with the security which I agree with the Prime Minister must ever be foremost in our minds in time of war which we all sincerely hope will never again eventuate. But I feel that the record deserves to have this statement of the events that have transpired since the introduction of the bill of rights, since the introduction of amendments to the War Measures Act similar to those in Bill C-62 introduced last session, similar to the amendments put forward in the bill of rights committee by Liberal members of the house to determine whether or not we can reconcile further with the bill of rights any act that is inconsistent or is a violation of our liberties and rights. These, it seems to me, are reasons that the government might well have expected us to express at this time.
I cannot explain why the government did not bring forward this measure earlier in the session other than the reasons I have given. They seem to be the only reasons in the light of all the facts that are apparent. 1 am sure that some hon. members, like the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and the 90205-6-396

Committee on War Measures Act because of being detained I missed the usual demonstration of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) laconism in introducing questions of this kind, his usual gems of language and his explanation of the legalities surrounding a problem of this nature. However, shortly after my arrival I was briefed by a fellow member as to what the Prime Minister had said so I think I have a very good idea of his remarks in introducing this motion.
I think everyone will realize that as a layman I suffer some disadvantage in following such legal luminaries as the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who are well versed in legal problems and constitutional matters. However, regardless of that I wish to assure the house that although I am a sort of simple, naive layman I have always had a great interest in this question and I fully realize and appreciate the purpose and the importance of this motion. While I am not able to discourse on the legal aspects of the question with any degree of knowledge compared with the previous speakers, I can say that I am one who always has been easily aroused by injustices and any transgression of human rights and human dignity has always concerned me.
In fact, over the years and until recent years I felt almost frustrated and exasperated on occasions at the lack of understanding of other persons' rights and I felt at times that I was tilting against windmills. I will say that I feel the situation in Canada has changed quite rapidly in recent years. More and more people are realizing what the citizen's rights are in a democratic state.
Like the previous speaker, I regret that this very important motion has been introduced at this late date in the session. The question is an important and serious one that requires time for almost leisurely study, shall I say. It is not one of those technical questions where you can deal with the matter with exactitude after certain facts have been produced. There is an infinite variety of aspects to a problem of this nature. Plenty of time must be taken for the hearing of views of legal authorities by the committee, for hearing the views of representatives of various sections of the community throughout the land and even the views of individuals who have paid a great deal of attention to this subject and have studied it for many years. Following the hearing of these views, I am sure the committee will require some time before it arrives at its conclusion.
This is a subject that will arouse a great deal of interest. As I said before, even in the smaller places I find that in recent years there is more interest in this topic than there was years ago. Years ago it was considered too

abstract, not in the ordinary day's activities, shall I say, but there is greater concern and interest now and the committee will need plenty of time to give consideration to the evidence, facts, views, suggestions and recommendations presented to it. Members of the house as individuals will want time to read the evidence and proceedings of the committee and I believe plenty of time should be provided. Later when legislation is introduced the house will want ample time to discuss this very important question properly and at suitable length. On that account I say again that we in this group regret that this motion was not introduced earlier in the session.
I am not going into the legal aspects of the matter. I am only going to deal with it from a broad point of view. As I said before, I am not competent to deal with the niceties of such a problem but I can deal with its impact on the citizen and speak of it in general terms. I believe that several advantages can flow from the passage of this motion, the study of the problem by the committee, by members of the house generally and the consequent proposed amendments to the War Measures Act. First of all, I think that the primary advantage is that the legislation will make certain, as far as it is humanly possible to do so under the circumstances, that the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens are protected in periods of emergency. I think that is the primary advantage.
Then I think there are two or three others. I believe that the gathering of evidence, facts, opinions, suggestions and recommendations from all those sectors of the Canadian community should prove of value to the present generation and to future generations. The record itself should prove of great value. Then I believe that the hearings of the committee and the discussion of the problem generally in the house and in the country will provide general interest in the subject and I am sure, as the result of happenings in recent years-[DOT] I am talking of happenings within the last ten or fifteen years, particularly since the second world war-greater understanding will be brought about. If the committee fulfils its responsibility and if the government accepts those recommendations which will come from people in all groups of society with various political opinions, including persons who support the group for which I have the honour to speak at the present time. I believe this whole study and consequent legislation will do something more to strengthen the sinews of democracy.
The average citizen is not learned in the law and is not learned in parliamentary procedure but he is interested in the basic rights of the citizen in a democracy. When you find

that this average citizen has a greater understanding, democracy is strengthened to that extent. We must realize that. While we are complacent and while we have accepted without question our freedom and our rights throughout the years, when we view the world around us it is marvellous to note how, under certain circumstances and certain emergency conditions, those rights can crumble if they are not supported by an informed citizenry.
In conclusion I wish to say that this group will co-operate in the work of the committee and in making suggestions as to amendments to the War Measures Act and will do all it can to the end that the demands of freedom and the rights of Canadian citizens are better served by this resolution, the consequent legislation and the action of this parliament. Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss this motion of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister
13, 1361
Committee on War Measures Act (Mr. Diefenbaker), which is one more evidence of the right hon. gentleman's real interest and determination to protect the rights and freedoms of the citizens of this country. It is one more step in the steady progress which has been made since the right hon. gentleman assumed the office of Prime Minister to undo the steady erosion of our rights and liberties which had taken place over the previous 22 years.
In discussing matters of this sort it is generally desirable to be calm and not to introduce notes of criticism. Of course, when dealing with intemperate speeches such as that of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) one recognizes that the hon. member gets carried away with a sense of his oratory, if not importance, and makes allowance for this kind of speech on that account. However, the hon. member did say something which I think calls for comment, because if there were no comment it would stand unanswered on the record of Hansard.
The first thing I wish to say simply by way of reply to my hon. friend is that he shows now a refreshing change of attitude from that which he showed during the many years he was a member of the treasury benches. Indeed, the government of which he was a part had 22 years in office during which time they had ample opportunity to deal with the War Measures Act and to remove from it those features which constitute the possibility, if not the fact, of an undue interference with human rights and fundamental freedoms. It was conspicuous then, and it is more conspicuous now in view of the hon. member's present attitude, that the previous administration did nothing during that time to bring about the results which the hon. member now professes himself so anxious to achieve.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when we listened this afternoon to the strictures heaped upon the government for not getting on with this proposal sooner, I think we are able to put the hon. gentleman's strictures in their proper perspective by recalling that his conversion, although we may welcome it, is very late.
The hon. member cannot take refuge in the answer that this measure is only necessary now because we did not have a bill of rights before; therefore his party and his government were blameless, because they did not have a bill of rights and it is the bill of rights that makes this necessary. It will be recalled that in the discussion of the bill of rights itself last year during all that lengthy period when we had to listen to the strictures he heaped upon that measure, he persisted in saying it added nothing by way of rights but was a mere codification of existing rights. If that is the hon. member's view, then the

Committee on War Measures Act rights which are in the bill of rights now existed at the time the hon. gentleman held office and the War Measures Act was as much in conflict with those rights then as it is now.
The hon. gentleman is now so anxious to see something done that he professes to claim exclusive credit for everything that is being done, yet, as I say, in all those years he was unable to see the importance of the measure which the Prime Minister has now brought forward. It is well understood, of course, that there is no one so keen as a recent convert and we welcome the hon. member to the ranks of the converted, the ranks of those who are now prepared to align themselves in support of the liberty of the individual. In contrast to the sudden conversion and the over eagerness now displayed by the hon. gentleman, may I emphasize that this government has been proceeding steadily and surely to the restoration and protection of those rights which were so eroded in earlier years. A major step was the enactment of the biU of rights itself. At that time the Prime Minister gave an undertaking that he would look at the War Measures Act and invite parliament to consider in what ways it might be amended so as to bring it into harmony with the bill of rights, and do what could be done to protect the rights of citizens even in times of emergency without unduly prejudicing the interests of the state as a whole.
Pursuant to the bill of rights we have brought in two important amendments to statutes this year to bring them into line with the bill of rights, and now comes this further measure initiated by the Prime Minister in order to make amends for the 22 years of erosion of rights-the motion we are now debating to set up a committee to examine the War Measures Act. Indeed, when one considers the change of attitude of the hon. member for Essex East I cannot help, while listening to him, thinking that he displays all the frustrated inconsistency which would be displayed by the outcome of a cross between a leopard and a chameleon, because you know, Mr. Speaker, the leopard's trouble is that he cannot change his spots while the chameleon changes colour with every perch upon which he alights. We come now to consider this motion which the hon. member professed a desire to see carried because that would have the result of amendments being made to the War Measures Act, and yet the hon. member has invited you, Mr. Speaker, to rule this motion out of order. Of course, with your usual wisdom and perspicacity you refused to entertain the point of order which the hon. member sought to raise, but the extraordinary thing to contemplate is this measure of frustration felt


by the hon. member for Essex East. He is so frustrated because he cannot himself claim the exclusive credit for what is being done that he forgets he has told us he intends to support the measure and solemnly invites Your Honour to rule it out of order. I think all members will understand the situation and accept the speech made by the hon. gentleman with the caution and reserve which it deserves.
What, then, of the proposal of the Prime Minister which is now before us, a proposal consistent with the undertaking which he gave last year when we were considering the bill of rights? This proposal, I suggest, sets out the proper way of dealing with this problem. The opposition has consistently suggested that we should get the bill of rights and the War Measures Act all mixed up and confused. Indeed, this desire on their part to confuse things was brought to my mind by one of the comments made by the hon. member for Essex East when he said the government had the habit of putting certain problems into one basket and certain other problems in another basket. He seemed to think this was a matter for criticism. It seems to me that this orderly method of dealing with things is the proper method instead of getting them all mixed up until, like the hon. member for Essex East, they are hopelessly confused. We have persistently and consistently taken the position that these matters should be dealt with separately because that is the most effective method of dealing with them.
When the bill of rights was before the special committee of the house last year there was a lengthy discussion on the bill in context with the War Measures Act and, as has been pointed out, one of the chief witnesses in this regard was Professor Lower of Queen's University. also significant to note that Professor Lower admitted the necessity for some legislation conferring special powers on the government in time of war.
