Mr. Speaker, the Farm Credit Act is very popular in British Columbia. Some 355 applications have been received and according to the latest figures there are 25 now pending. To date about 16 per cent of the applications have been rejected. The total amount of loans in British Columbia is $3,469,150 for some 254 loans, or an average of about $13,700 per loan. I believe that Fraser Valley tops the list in the province for the number of loans made with the Okanagan Boundary district coming second.
As Fraser Valley is the centre of a large dairy industry, it is an area where farm loans are often required. The large co-operative Fraser Valley milk producers' association does big business in this area amounting to some $27 million a year. High-class cattle are bred here and although sales there do not average as high as the figure of $1,790, which was reached in Ontario recently at the national sale, the cattle that are bred do furnish considerable revenue along with the revenue from milk production.
I had one rejection of a loan brought to my attention before I came here last fall. A young man had received a farm of 225 acres with excellent soil because of the death of his mother and he wanted to borrow $20,000 on the farm. There were no mortgages on the farm at the time and I was rather amazed when he telephoned me one day and said that

his loan application had been refused. I discussed the matter with the supervisor and he informed me that he considered that this man was trying to run an uneconomic operation. There were two hired men on the farm in addition to the owner and they were milking 30 cows. It is a poor man these days who cannot milk 30 cows himself, let alone having three men doing the job. This application was turned down but the young man then borrowed the money privately elsewhere.
In discussing the Farm Credit Act I think we should consider both the pros and cons, and if I am a little critical I hope the minister will forgive me. It may be because of the hot, sultry weather we are having but I do feel somewhat critical tonight about certain features of the act. I believe the chief criticism of the act in British Columbia is the difficulty of getting a loan on a small acreage, say 10 acres. Holdings of that size may be operated as poultry, berry, vegetable, flower, seed or even holly farms. A poultryman does not require heavy, fertile soil. In fact, for drainage purposes often poorer soil is better than rich soil. On the other hand, a berry crop requires a good soil. These are opposite situations but it shows the difference that can be found in 10-acre farms. It is amazing how much a revenue can be derived from 10 acres under certain circumstances.
I believe that at the commencement of the operation of the act the idea was that a poultryman should produce on the property half the feed that he uses. Hence he needed more than just a small acreage and this was one of the reasons why applications were turned down. This is an erroneous idea. Grain may be purchased in Fraser valley and in fact in most of British Columbia much more cheaply than it can be grown, especially on small farms and crop failures could be common especially in wet weather. This is a very poor idea but if my information is correct, at the present time I believe this clause has now been more or less eliminated and it is up to the supervisor as to whether he thinks there is a prospect of this particular farmer, whether he is a poultryman, a dairyman, or a fruit grower, can make a success of the venture.
The small dairy farmer is a different proposition. So, as I say, anything that has a reasonable chance of success is likely to be passed by the supervisor. A loan on a farm that is not operating successfully should be turned down anyway. Where farmers cannot succeed, it is often necessary to move or at least for the sons to seek employment elsewhere.
This is where vocational training schools fit into the picture of the farm loan board.
90205-6-398J
Farm Credit Act
The vocational training school project has gradually caught fire. I note that Ontario is planning an $8 million building program to be completed during the next year and a half. This will accommodate many students from farms as well as other places and even the actual labour of building will, it is stated, provide employment for about 20,000 workers for 18 months. In a local paper from British Columbia recently I noted a report stating that the minister of education has planned to spend $10 million on enlarging vocational schools in agricultural areas in order to look after certain instruction to young farmers and farmers' daughters. Some farms in British Columbia are well adapted for recreation centres around a lake or for motels or camp sites, et cetera. A dude ranch might be more profitable than is more standard farming. This whole system is suitable for arranging just such things as these. All these features should be investigated by the owner in order to see whether increased revenue, some of it easy money, could not be picked up. If failure is sure on any farm, no loan should be given.
Another criticism in Fraser valley and the coast area occurred when the provincial head office was moved from New Westminster to Kelowna. It was moved without notice and to the minds of many, for very little reason. It was asserted that it was nearer the centre of British Columbia. This is incorrect because Vanderhoof is the centre of the province. It was asserted that there were more loans in this area. I believe this statement was incorrect. It was asserted that it was nearer the farming area. May I say that Fraser Valley produces a great deal of farm revenue. I am sure there is agreement on that matter. It was asserted that it was easier of access. This assertion I again contend is false. If you wanted to fly to Kelowna from here, you would go to Vancouver and fly back-

Mr. Speaker, last night when we listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) speak and again tonight I think we realized that he gave a rather concise picture of the operation of the farm credit corporation and of the need to increase the authorized capital of the corporation itself. Those of us who represent farm constituencies realize at first hand the need for this increase in capital because of the great demand for the service which the corporation is rendering. In an area such as that which I represent, where the assessment ranges from $500 a quarter section to $5,000, you can well realize the difficulty in the operation, and the assessment and the appraisal of the applications which come in. However, I have been greatly impressed by the enthusiasm not only of the staff and the officials of the farm credit corporation but by the responsibility which the applicants feel towards the officials of the farm credit corporation. It makes a person realize that the staff and the officials who are administering the act and working for the corporation really believe in them wholeheartedly. They impress upon the applicants the possibilities which are theirs within the scope of the act and the great way in which the farmers can avail themselves of the various opportunities.
When we look at the figures very briefly for the last three years, Mr. Speaker, we can realize why this authorization is required. In 1958, when the farm loan board was in effect, the loans made that year amounted to $30 million. In the following year, when the farm loan board was operated and the farm credit corporation took over after October 5, the loans rose to $40 million. In this last year for which we have records the loans are up to $60 million.
There has been very little increase in the staff during those three years. It is fairly obvious that the services which are rendered by the staff of the farm credit corporation are really outstanding. I refer primarily to the pre-loan counselling which is given by the farm credit corporation advisers. These officials are devoted servants. They are intelligent and they certainly have dedication to the work which they are doing. As I say, they impress the farmers very greatly and they are able to interpret the provisions of the

act in a most admirable manner. The farmers who benefit by the clauses of the act realize that here is something which can improve their position. They are now able to get adequate credit which for many years had been denied them. They are aware that under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture we have a corporation which is serving a crying need that had been denied for a long time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see the evening is wearing on and in rising at this time it is not my purpose to delay the second reading of this bill. However, I do have some brief comments to make on farm credit legislation.
I think that before looking at Canada's new farm credit legislation we might look at the farm credit situation as it existed prior to the introduction of these measures, and at some of the reasons why legislative changes appeared necessary if agriculture was to be given a chance to take advantage of the new technologies and methods which have been found so effective in reducing agricultural costs.
The amount of capital required to set up a minimum economic family farm unit having more than doubled since the last war, the credit arrangements which could be made under the Canadian farm loan act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, either separately or together, although fairly adequate for the well established farmer were entirely inadequate to meet the needs of the young and capable farmer desirous of setting up an economic family farm unit unless, of course, he was fortunate enough to possess at least 50 per cent of the required capital or a minimum of $15,000.
To start out with something less than an economic family farm unit meant higher production costs in the beginning, and consequently very little by way of profit with which to expand. The struggle toward such a unit had become so slow that only a fortunate few ever reached it in time to fully exploit its advantages and, because of its cost, it was a difficult unit to dispose of in its entirety or even to transfer from one generation to another without the intervention of very substantial credit. The result has been that the transition to the family farm unit of economic size capable of using modern methods and of producing a standard, readily marketable product at a minimum cost has, in most parts of this country, been extremely slow.
There seemed to be good reason to believe that the problems associated with low farm income and with surplus disposal were closely linked with relatively high production costs,

and that these excess costs were largely due to the fact that by far the greater number of Canadian farms were still a long way from being economic units by present day standards. It also seemed evident that lack of capital was making it difficult for farmers in the more adaptable areas to switch production from straight grain farming and in so doing help bring production more in line with future market requirements as estimated by the Gordon commission on Canada's economic future.
With our rangeland potential almost fully exploited, the predicted large increase in the demand for beef would have to be met in our more adaptable cultivated areas, both east and west, through switching to grassland farming and, incidentally, putting more of our good land into effective preservation against the day when every available acre may have to be put under intensive cultivation in order to feed our own increasing population and high protein foods, such as beef, will be a luxury, as they are today in many parts of the world.
That the net income of competent farmers now on inadequate units could be increased by at least 50 per cent and their production made to conform more nearly to future market requirements with ample, long term, package deal credit made available to them was well established by a survey conducted by the Veterans' Land Act administration in 1958.
This survey covered a cross section of 25 per cent of Veterans' Land Act farm settlers in all provinces of Canada and was made for the purpose of assessing their future credit requirements. It was also so designed that it would show what effect the availability and use of adequate long term credit would have on their farm income and on their future production pattern, they having been previously exposed to at least some instruction having to do with modern farm organization and methods, particularly as applied to agriculture, through the services provided by federal farm credit advisers.
The results of this survey indicated that the most serious problems facing agriculture today may well stem from the lack of sufficient long term credit. It also seemed evident that ample, long term, package deal credit designed to assist competent young farmers in the setting up of family farm units of economic size, when granted in sufficient amounts to do the job for which it was intended, always enough but never too much, was probably the most effective and economical way in which the government could assist agriculture to attain parity of income with other industries, and this through the
Farm Credit Act
medium of reduced production costs from which the whole economy would benefit.
While this would be essentially a long term program, the assembly under a competent owner-operator of each and every new, economically sized family farm unit would bring agriculture one step nearer to the objective of parity income for its operators and production costs which would not only keep the home market but would make it possible to compete favourably in the export market as well.
The object of this legislation, as stated by the then minister of agriculture, is:
-to assist Canadian farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into economic family farm units, each of which will be of sufficient size or efficiency to produce the farm income necessary to pay all operating and maintenance costs; to provide a good livelihood for the owner-operator and his dependents; and to retire any required credit, with interest, within an appropriate term.
There are several reasons why this new credit program should be better than the old, the most important being that the corporation is operating under more comprehensive and forward looking credit legislation, with policy directed specifically toward the task of assisting the industry to reorganize itself into sound, economic family farm units.
Next in importance is the fact that the corporation has at its all-important field level a force of over 200 trained and experienced resident credit advisers who are now well deployed throughout the agricultural areas of the country. These have been drawn largely from trained and experienced V.L.A. farm credit advisers.
There is one area in the farm credit field that I feel merits careful consideration. In Manitoba, particularly, the size of the farm is not always a criterion for establishing an economic unit. I am advised by the farm credit corporation officials that it is the income potential rather than the unit size that provides a basis for their lending policy.
Where proper rotation, and careful husbandry is used, a loan to modernize equipment, or intensify the operation of the holding would be as satisfactory for increasing incomes as would a loan to enlarge the farm.
All farmers do not want to be big time operators. Many prefer to manage successfully on a small, but productive unit.
The fact that the farm credit corporation is seeking additional funds suggests that its credit facilities are being administered successfully under careful appraisal and supervision.
The continued use of these credit facilities by our farm people should have an important bearing on the income improvement of our rural communities, and the continuation of

Farm. Credit Act
the family farm, which is so essential to the economic well-being of the nation.

speechtext:
No. I should like to say a few words before the house passes this bill. The Farm Credit Act has been a matter of concern to me over the years and it has also been of concern to my constituents. The measure before us is designed to increase the amount which can be loaned under the act. It increases the amount of capital from $8 million to $12 million and as a result of the multiplication factor involved an additional $100 million will be made available for lending under the act.
This bill is a necessity because at the present time $165 million has been lent out and only $200 million can be lent, so before the end of the year the amount will have to be increased. We are now increasing it to $300 million. While discussing the total amount available for lending under the act I might point out that this government took action in 1958, under the old farm credit act, but $80 million was the limit of the amount which could be lent under it. In 1958 we increased the amount available under the farm credit act to $120 million but we saw the need for a still further increase and today the present bill will provide for $300 million to be lent out to farmers.
I may say that the act has worked reasonably well in most parts of Canada and perhaps in a large part of my own constituency but in my own constituency and in other parts of western Canada including northern and southern Alberta there are areas which are known as local improvement districts. These have certain special characteristics and the act as it now stands does not lend itself too readily to providing assistance in these particular areas. In my own constituency there are areas known as "special areas" somewhat similar in character to local improvement districts and here again the act as it now stands is not well adapted to the making of loans in those areas. I mentioned this in my maiden speech in 1958. Up until 1958, under the old act, there were no loans made in those particular areas. I may say there are about 3,000 farmers living in those areas and there is a demand for land and there is a change-over of land; this has been particularly the case in the last few years.
Again, the act may not be working too well in connection with the smaller farms as the minister himself suggested when he spoke this afternoon. I am thinking particularly of a case which was brought to my attention where a

farmer had been farming for the last ten or 15 years since the war on what we would call a small holding. He saw an opportunity to buy another quarter section recently adjoining his farmstead. He applied for a loan and his application was turned down because they thought his farm was not of an economic size. They said: if instead of $4,000 you are prepared to borrow $20,000 and buy an economic unit we will lend you the money, but we will not lend you $4,000. This particular farmer had been farming for 13 years He was a young man who had started farming in 1948 and who had acquired a lot of machinery, and perhaps a few debts with it, but he had been able to sustain himself and his family on a section of land. I think in this particular case he had a section and a quarter, and he had a lease on another half section. He wanted to buy another quarter section which he could have obtained for $4,000 but the corporation turned him down and said: you look around and try to find a large farm that is worth $20,000 and we will lend you the money.
These are some of the difficulties I have found in connection with the administration of this act. This particular farmer does not wish to move from his present farm. He wanted to add to it as adjacent land became available. Had he bought the other quarter section he might not have been through adding to it. He might have continued to add to it from year to year and maybe at the end of five or six years he would have built his loan up to $20,000. I think the corporation should have taken into consideration the fact that this particular farmer had been existing on his farm site. He wanted to add to his land as property became available. It is true he might not have had what some persons would consider to be an economic unit but we all know the difficulty of defining an economic unit. Acreage certainly enters into it, but acreage is not the only factor. It depends on how intensively the acreage is farmed. So I hope the men in charge of the administration of this act will pay particular attention to these things. I note that other hon. members who have spoken in connection with this measure tonight have encountered situations where this idea of what constitutes an economic unit in a given area sometimes varies to a large extent according to the peculiarities of a given locality. I certainly think there is a great deal of variation in what constitutes an economic unit and how it should be appraised in any particular area.
The particular areas I mentioned a while ago, the "special areas", are generally considered by some to be ranching country. But

there are lots of good farming spots in central Alberta-lots of places where the farmer can sustain himself and his family on a section and a half or two sections of land. In other areas he may need closer to ten sections. So I hope the authorities will be more ready to lend a small sum of money rather than trying to encourage young farmers to borrow the largest amounts in order to buy well established farms. It is today very difficult to find a well established farm or what most individuals would consider to be an economic unit, for less than $20,000. I think the farmer who wishes to enlarge, develop or perhaps intensify his farm operations, should surely be able to do so with credit obtained under this particular measure.
The minister made brief reference to the suggestion of accepting leased land as security for loans made under this act. I should like to enlarge upon that subject.
In my particular area the farmers have had a great deal of difficulty in using leased land as security for loans under the act. I realize that authorities have suggested that a loan on this basis could qualify under part III of the act as it now stands. However, I should like to point out that under part III of the act a potential borrower cannot purchase land in respect to which he is a tenant farmer. I can see no reason why the farm credit corporation should not accept a lease in its name, allowing a farmer to borrow money in order to develop that land until he has paid the loan, at which time the lease would then revert to his own name.
In a great many areas of southwestern Saskatchewan, southeastern Alberta, and even the southwestern portion of Alberta along the foothills, a great deal of leased land is used for agricultural purposes. In my particular area leases change hands at the rate of $3 to $6 per acre. That is not a lot of money, and certainly a farmer would not have to borrow much money under this act to buy land of that type at that price, and would be in a position to repay the loan within a relatively short period of time. If the farmer had enough livestock he could use that as security for a loan under the farm credit corporation measure along with his leased land, put in the name of the corporation, and would then find himself in a position to pay back the loan within a few years, at which time the lease would revert to his own name. I understand that the Veterans' Land Act administration has worked closely with the farm credit corporation administration. I should like to point out to the minister that I am aware of certain cases where the Veterans' Land Act administration has accepted leases in its name as
Farm Credit Act
security for loans. I suggest this same practice could be followed by the administration of this act.
There has been some mention made during the debate this afternoon of the subsidization provided under this act. The idea has been expressed that there might be a continued subsidization in this regard. I take strong exception to those suggestions, because last year was the first year for a long period of time that the farm credit corporation, or the farm loans act, lost money.
The government is now in a position to borrow money from the Bank of Canada, if I read the figures correctly, at an interest rate of between 3.3 per cent and 4 per cent. I say that because of articles appearing in various newspapers recently. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) frowning at me. Perhaps the interest rate is 3.30 per cent.
In any event the interest rate is between 3 per cent and 4 per cent. In view of that fact, I see no reason why the government cannot borrow money at that interest rate, and make loans under this act to farmers because, as the minister stated last night, the operation cost amounted to only .8 per cent. Under this act, borrowers must pay 5 per cent interest, so that even if the government had to pay 4 per cent on its borrowings, it could do so and make these loans at a profit.
For the reasons I have set out, I cannot understand why this measure is considered to be a subsidization at all.
Some hon. members might feel that this particular measure does not concern the farmers in my area. I should like to point out that under section 27 of the act a loan can be made to cover a complete farming operation, using the farmers chattels as security, only if the loan is made under part III of the act. In addition, there are further stipulations which must be met. The first important stipulation is that a farmer cannot borrow, under part III of the act, at the same time as he has a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. As an example of the difficulty involved here I should cite the case of a farmer farming an area, who desires to purchase additional land through a loan under part III of the act. Having done so, he would be prohibited from borrowing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in order to purchase new or additional machinery to farm his land. While there may be a few isolated cases where an individual has used the same piece of machinery as security for two different loans, I see no difficulty in that regard under the application of part III, because when a young farmer makes application to the bank for a loan under the Farm

Farm Credit Act
Improvement Loans Act, the banker makes absolutely sure that the machinery used as security is clear of encumbrances.
I suggest the individuals who will take advantage of the loans available under this new legislation will be young fanners with a desire to purchase their father's holdings, and will be required to borrow close to the maximum amount. If those individuals accept supervision, they would make loans under part III of this act. Having done so they would not then be able to borrow money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act to purchase additional machinery, until such time as the original loan was reduced to less than $20,000. I can foresee complications arising because of the application of part III, and I do not understand the reason for its inclusion in the act.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to touch upon one other subject before I conclude, having to do with the appraisal fee. Most hon. members are perhaps aware that the appraisal fee is now set at 2 per cent of the amount of the loan, or $100, whichever is the lesser. I feel it is unnecessary to increase this appraisal fee from $10 to $100. I suggest this has caused a great deal of concern and hardship to those farmers who must pay the $100 appraisal fee in addition to the cost of finding out whether the title to the land is clear. I suggest that the total cost to the farmer, when making application for a loan under this measure, including the appraisal fee, might well be $200. That fact in itself perhaps would not be such a great problem if there was any assurance to the farmer that, having paid out that money, his application would be approved. In some instances farmers are apt to have an appraisal made, pay $100 and be turned down after the appraisal is made. Although the farmer is turned down, he still has to pay the $100. This is a hardship on a particular farmer who is thus prevented from enlarging his present holdings, as was the case in the instance I mentioned earlier this evening.
I should like to see some changes made in this regulation, perhaps not at this session but in the year to come, and the appraisal fee be reduced to $10 as it was formerly. If the applicant is turned down, or if the appraisal is not made, the fee should be refunded. This is a small point but I thought I should mention it because I know some of the difficulties that some farmers have had in my constituency in trying to get loans under this particular act. I might say that only the one area in my constituency has had this trouble. Farmers in this area have been turned down on a number of occasions because, as I said, they did not want to borrow too much money. They just wanted to

borrow a little to add to their present holdings. Sometimes an appraiser would come into the drier part of Alberta and not recommend the loan. The country is dry, so much so that some people have claimed the gophers have moved out. Actually it is not that bad. Farmers in that particular area are as good security risks as farmers in any other part of the province. They have proved this over the years.
I would strongly recommend that an appraiser be placed in this particular area because of the number of applicants that have been turned down. An appraiser coming from some of the more fertile parts of Alberta, the parts fortunate enough to receive a great deal of rain, drives into this dry country and says, "Oh my gosh, I would not lend a plugged nickel in this country", and drives out again. A farmer trying to borrow some money is put in the position where his case is not properly viewed in the light that perhaps he would hope it would be, and he is turned down almost automatically because he is living in that particular area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see this change and I should like to say a few words on the bill.
So far as I can ascertain, the remarks that have been made so far have all been in favour of this legislation. The reason that we are in favour of the increase in the amount of money is that there has been a new director appointed under the Farm Credit Act. We should be appreciative of the job he has been able to do in such a short time. The fact that we need more money under the Farm Credit Act now is an indication that the act is working for the first time in a long period of time.
It has always seemed to me that borrowing money from the Canadian farm loan board was a little bit like trying to borrow money from the treasury board or going to the Minister of Finance and asking him for a loan. The administrators of the act were not the least bit interested in lending money. There were certain requirements. If you fitted into that particular limited pattern then you got the money. Mr. Rutherford, the former director of the Veterans' Land Act did have experience. His officials had the approach of wanting to lend money that was going to be advantageous to the farmers. You did not lend the money whether the person needed it or not. Previously it depended on whether the farmer fitted into a little slot. It did not depend necessarily on whether it was advantageous to the farmer; he got the money if he met certain requirements. Now it seems no matter whether the money is asked for under
Farm Credit Act
supervision or not there is continuously a certain amount of supervision. It seems to me this is the only way that money being lent to farmers is going to be advantageously used by those farmers. Although farmers may not readily admit it, they need assistance in ascertaining how much help they need. The hon. member who just took his seat spoke of areas of 10,000 acres. This certainly does not apply in my area.

I am sorry if I misquoted the hon. member. It would not make any difference. Ten sections are still a great deal more than the area on which farmers in my constituency are going to be borrowing money, if it is a very large amount of land. It has been a factor. I presume the hon. member was referring to the need for larger farms to make up an economic unit. There has been a tendency for farmers to borrow money on an uneconomical unit. Obviously his borrowing of that money was not going to enable him to better his position very much.
One of the things to the credit of the Veterans' Land Act administration was the ability of the officials to supervise and the advice they gave. This practice is now being applied generally to Canadian farm loans and it means that the farmer is receiving some assistance and technical advice that he did not have the opportunity to obtain before. The advice is being given in such a manner that the farmer will accept it because it is not completely dependent upon the loan or the conditions of the loan. In my area, for example, farmers have been advised that if they plant certain crops the market is such and such and if they plant something else their chances of obtaining a better price per acre of produce will be much more readily realized. In some instances technical advice has been given in relation to the operation of the farm.
It seems to me that the technical assistance being given in this way by the officials is a great advantage over the system that obtained before. The Farm Credit Act agents are going to the farms and talking to the farmer and his wife. They are assessing the situation themselves and in my opinion this is doing a great deal to enable the farmer to obtain an advantageous loan, one which he is going to be able to repay and which it is to his advantage to obtain.
The fact that the government is asking for an increase in the amount of money available for loans is an indication that this credit system is an advantageous one. With its experience under this act, I believe that the

Farm Credit Act
government is going to give consideration to increasing the supervision under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. There is a similarity between the two acts. As a previous speaker mentioned, they are interrelated to some extent and they certainly work advantageously in combination.
Having in mind the inquiry into farm machinery that is now under way, I believe it is increasingly advantageous for the farmer to have impartial advice with relation to the purchase of new machinery because occasionally we find that rather than the farmer wanting to buy, the machinery companies are persuading him to buy. A little advice may help to prevent some farmers from trying to keep up with the Jones'. It seems to me that this act is a credit to the government. We are very pleased with the way it has been operating and with the fact that more money is necessary. We are also pleased that the bill has been introduced and will be passed before the budget is brought down because it might be more difficult at that time.

Twenty-four Canadian parliamentarians attending an interparliamentary meeting in Washington last week agreed with their United States colleagues that nuclear weapons should be used if necessary to defend West Berlin.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext:
In accordance with the regular practice I wish to announce the appointment of the deputy postmaster general, effective
June 20. Mr. William Hugh Wilson is to fill the vacancy resulting from the forthcoming retirement of Mr. George A. Boyle, who has served for 45 years.
I should like to express appreciation on behalf of the government for the service Mr. Boyle has rendered. He has made many outstanding contributions to the development of Canada's postal service, particularly in the field of international postal affairs where he has represented Canada as vice-president of the executive and liaison committee of the universal postal union.
Mr. Wilson has been director of operations in the head office of the department since April, 1959. He entered the post office in 1929 as a temporary postal helper in Vancouver. He became postmaster in Vancouver in 1955, and in 1958 was named regional director of postal service for the Pacific region.
Mr. Wilson brings to the position of deputy postmaster general outstanding administrative skill and unusual ability to achieve results while maintaining the support of those who work for him. He has been responsible for numerous major innovations in postal techniques. As director of operations he has been responsible for all the aspects of the day to day operation of the postal service except matters of transportation.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON EXCHANGE OF LEAD FOR SURPLUS U.S. GRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: STATEMENT ON EXCHANGE OF LEAD FOR SURPLUS U.S. GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, June 9, I undertook to take as notice the question raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia as to whether the reported transaction between the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada and the United States authorities, involving the barter of Canadian lead for United States grain, would have any effect on Canada's own grain marketing policy.
I have now been informed that this transaction has been concluded and that it does not depart from the pattern of previous barter transactions entered into by the United States authorities in obtaining primary or strategic commodities under public law 480. From the government's standpoint this is a private business transaction concluded by a private Canadian firm and, as the hon. member is aware, the government does not interfere in private business transactions. Our only concern is that the sale of surplus grain thus acquired through barter will not displace normal commercial sales of grain. On this point we have been assured that this barter transaction will be subject to the same safeguards as those already established and agreed upon, and which have been applied in the past for the protection of our commercial marketing areas.

subsubtopic: REPORTED EXPOSURE OF CHILDREN TO RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 10 the hon. member for Assiniboia asked for my comments in connection with a recent incident in Toronto in which children were in contact with some powder containing radium, which they discovered in a warehouse.
I should like to pay tribute to the prompt and efficient manner in which the local authorities acted, which seems to have averted the danger of any serious results. On the basis of all the information received there seems to be no reason to expect that any of the persons involved will suffer any ill effects. The last stages of the clean-up and accounting process are now going on under the immediate direction of officers of the Ontario department of health.
During world war II large amounts of radium powder were used to paint luminous dials in aircraft and other equipment. It seems clear that the supplies in this case came from that source and were obtained before 1947, when the regulations of the atomic energy control board came into effect. Such material cannot now be acquired except under licence from the board, and licences are not granted unless the board is satisfied, on the advice of its health advisers, that the recipient has adequate knowledge and facilities to ensure that no health hazard will result.
It may be that some of the radium powder obtained prior to 1947 is still stored in industrial establishments, warehouses and similar places. After so many years the material will have lost its usefulness for the painting of luminous dials, but it will remain a potential danger to health because of its radioactivity. I wish, therefore, to advise all organizations to make quite sure that they do not have in storage any old stocks of radium luminous compound. My colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, whose department advises the atomic energy control board on matters relating to health and safety, suggests that the radiation protection division of his department be notified if any such material is found. That division

can then make arrangements for proper disposal, which should not be attempted by other parties.
Meanwhile, every effort is being made to locate any other supplies that may still be in existence under similar circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I was unavoidably absent yesterday afternoon when the bill was considered on second reading and in committee.
I should like now to give the reasons that would have prompted me to take exception, not to the bill itself, but to section 15 in particular.
On account of that section, numerous representations were submitted to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, when the latter examined the bill, by the St. Lawrence pilots' federation and other organizations.
It now seems obvious that since 1959, that is, since Bill S-3 was introduced, the government has never given up the idea of eventually abolishing pilotage on the St. Lawrence.

(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, in 1959, following representations made by various pilots' associations and several members of parliament, the then minister of transport withdrew Bill S-3 to exempt any ship designated by the governor in council from the obligation of paying pilotage dues.
The government undoubtedly realized that their action was too drastic and they decided to proceed by steps but, I repeat, always with a view to abolishing pilotage all along the St. Lawrence.
That, in my opinion, is why section 15 was inserted in the bill we now have before us.
Indeed, section 15 stipulates that American lakers will be exempt from the obligation of paying pilotage dues in the St. Regis district down to Montreal, that is in an exclusively Canadian zone.
The scheme is clever. The exemption is only for that section for the time being but, in a few years from now, it will be extended to the whole length of the river.
Canada Shipping Act
The minister may tell us, as he did before the committee, that it will not be so. I am quite willing to take his word for it but, on the other hand, he will agree with me that his statement binds neither his successor nor the government.
The assurance he has given to the committee is no guarantee for the pilots as far as the future is concerned.
When this bill was examined in committee, we had the opportunity of hearing the legal adviser of the St. Lawrence pilots' federation and the representative of the Canadian merchant service guild.
These two representatives indicated before the committee that they took particular exception to clause 15 first on grounds of national sovereignty and then on grounds of safety in navigation.
The matter of sovereignty and of treaties was clearly dealt with yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I will not therefore take it up again.
As for the question of safety, it must first be recognized that with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, the traffic is bound to increase considerably in the coming years. Moreover, as the ships plying those waters will be bigger and speedier, the danger will be greater. The logical thing to do then, Mr. Speaker, is to render more stringent the safety measures, not to relax them. As a matter of fact, that is what we have been doing for several years now in the case of highways. In order to insure the greatest safety on our highways, the traffic laws have been tightened each year.
When asked by the members of the committee to comment upon the conditions of navigation in the district concerned, Mr. Guy Chartier, president of the Cornwall district pilot association, stated that the channel was quite narrow and difficult. He added that in his opinion no one should be allowed to pilot a ship in those waters unless he had been plying them for six or seven years. He also remarked that on the Canadian side, before getting a pilot licence, one had to have a master licence and two years of navigation in this area after apprenticeship while, on the American side, licence is granted after 12 trips only, which gave him reason to conclude unhesitatingly that such persons could not be qualified to navigate in that district.

Would my hon. friend allow me a question?

Canada Shipping Act
Surely.
Is he not aware that it is absolutely forbidden to any American pilot to pilot a ship in Canadian waters, between St. Regis and Montreal?

Yes, but is the minister not aware also that, under the amendment to section 15, captains of United States ships shall not be required to take a pilot on board and that, according to the statement made in Montreal by the president of the federation or association of the St. Regis district pilots, after 12 trips masters or captains will to be able to obtain a certificate allowing them to pilot their ships from Cornwall to Montreal. Therefore, I base my assertion on the statement made by the president of the association of pilots.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This allows the Americans to pilot their ships without the help of a Canadian pilot.
This is the argument of the hon. member for Laurier: under section 15, United States ships may now ply from Cornwall to Montreal without the help of a Canadian pilot.
They could do it before.

I admit they could do it before, but circumstances were different, as the hon. member for Laurier mentioned when he discussed that point.
I wish to point out, that it is strange that the Department of Transport does not require the American masters-and I repeat the point the minister and I just mentioned-to pass tests before they are permitted to pilot their ships in exclusively Canadian waters. It seems to me that we should expect from the American masters the same qualifications and the same degree of experience as we expect from our own pilots.
Therefore, it seems clear to me according to the views of experienced men, that to exempt those ships of the payment of pilotage dues would endanger the safety of navigation in that area. Furthermore, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, the adoption of clause 15 would be a step toward the abolition of compulsory pilotage by Canadian pilots in the other districts of the St. Lawrence river.
The minister is aware that strong representations have been made in Washington- and there is no call to doubt their continuance in the future-to grant the American lakers the same privileges upon the whole length of the St. Lawrence river.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that it was for those reasons that I would have supported

yesterday the amendment of the hon. member for Laurier to the effect that clause 15 of the bill be deleted.
I regret very much that the minister refused to agree to that amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it was suggested during the committee stage of this bill that Canada had given up something but had not received in return a quid pro quo. I should like to deal with that point for just a moment or two.
I should like to refer to pages 1 and 2 of the treaty between Canada and the United States dated May 5, 1961. At page 1 it is provided that the President of the United States by proclamation may declare certain areas compulsory pilotage areas, and listed there are districts Nos. 1, 2 and 3. Without reading the detailed descriptions, district No. 1 is the St. Lawrence area between St. Regis and Kingston, district No. 2 is roughly the area of the St. Clair river, and, district No. 3 is the area of the St. Mary's river and Sault Ste. Marie.
I should like to read the paragraph following the description of those districts, which is as follows:
Registered vessels of the United States and foreign vessels navigating United States waters of the great lakes which are not designated by the president by proclamation-
That refers to the three preceding areas that have been designated. I continue:
-are required by the act to have on board a United States registered pilot or a Canadian registered pilot or other officer qualified for the waters concerned

To me, and I think to anyone who reads it, that is a clear indication that Canada does receive some rights in United States waters and the great lakes, particularly the waters of lake Michigan.
There was a question asked in the committee as to why this matter of having a pilot or not having a pilot betweeen St. Regis and Montreal was not covered by the treaty. One answer is that the waters are exclusively Canadian. I think perhaps an analogy can be made regarding the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. In order to make a workable navigation seaway in Canada, certain work had to be done on the canals between St. Regis and Montreal. That work was done at a cost to and by the Canadian government because it is exclusively Canadian waters. Would the United States government have spent the $100 million odd it did spend without having the assurance from the Canadian government that it was going to improve the channel between St. Regis and Montreal?

I think the analogy is clear there. The United States government would not have given us a general pilotage agreement concerning the whole of the St. Lawrence system without having received an undertaking or understanding that certain provisions would be made for it in respect to that section of the St. Lawrence seaway from St. Regis to Montreal.
I am not sure that the argument of the hon. member for Levis is valid when he says this is only a first step. I cannot go as far as he does, because it seems to me quite clear that Montreal is the end of the seaway works built either by Canada or the United States, and there would be no validity in a United States request for pilotage rights beyond Montreal by reason of that fact. It is true, of course, that the traffic between the United States and Canada, in that section from Seven Islands to the Ohio steel ports on the United States side, is increasing and that possibly fewer ships than heretofore will now turn around at Montreal, although I think for some years Montreal will be essentially the eastern terminal of the seaway in regard to grain shipments.
Again I should like to emphasize the fact that there has not been any clear indication as to the matter of safety. Sometimes we tend to make open assumptions that when an accident happened at a time when there was no pilot on board, it happened because there was no pilot on board. I do not think our pilots would be happy if we made the similar assumption that because there was a pilot on board at the time an accident happened, it was his fault. As I pointed out in committee, I hope better statistics and records are kept so that more detailed statistics can be published. If this is done we will then have the opportunity of assessing that portion of responsibility for an accident which is attributable to the fact that a pilot was not on board.

Mr. Speaker, I do not seek to raise a new debate or continue the one we had yesterday, but just the same, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) has raised some points that have to be considered and to which I must make some correction.
First of all, for the hon. member's information, I should tell him that the Department of Transport gives the St. Lawrence pilots a remarkably good treatment. In fact,
I think there are few Canadian corporations whose employees are so highly paid proportionately to their work. I realize that pilots have responsibilities, and my department has always seen to it that their salaries or dues be guaranteed and in line with their responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing we seem to forget sometimes about our pilots: our primary concern should be the safety of navigation on the St. Lawrence river. On the other hand, if we impose all sorts of charges and give rise to all sorts of difficulties, if, in a word, we enforce special procedures for vessels using the St. Lawrence river, there is a risk of less efficiency in the St. Lawrence shipping trade.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in our discussion with the United States, in order to come to some agreement with regard to piloting on the great lakes or any other waterway where both countries have a common interest, we must keep in mind that the safety of navigation must be the prime consideration. The same applies to the efficiency of seaway traffic. We do not wish ships to be hampered in their business; on the contrary, they should be able to go about their business in a logical way. That is why, in those discussions with the United States, we always have in mind not only the improvement of seaway traffic but also the protection of the Canadian pilots' position, their salaries and the part they play in the seaway traffic of this country.
That is why in this case, when we had to negotiate with the United States, we came to an agreement which, to my mind, is justified. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) explained a

Canada Shipping Act
moment ago, the Americans also made some concessions, and I am convinced that the agreement which has been concluded is entirely reasonable, as not a single Canadian pilot will lose a cent because American vessels benefit from an exemption. Not a single Canadian pilot will lose his job following this arrangement, because we did insist that no American pilot be entitled to do any piloting on the St. Lawrence river, between St. Regis and Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Levis suggested a moment ago that the Department of Transport did not seem to care too much about the fate of our Canadian pilots, and that our officials seemed to want to please the Americans. Well, I must point out to him that the Department of Transport guarantees very attractive salaries to the pilots, and that there are not many Canadian corporations which pay their staff a salary of about $12,000 a year, not including an expense allowance of up to a couple of thousand dollars, and all that for eight or nine months of work.
I know Canadian pilots have responsibilities and that their services are most important to shipping and in many other ways. Just the same, they are paid very attractive salaries. Members of the Canadian corporation of pilots enjoy rights based on an ancient tradition which I respect as much as anyone else; however, in view of the fact that the Department of Transport guarantees jobs and fees to Canadian pilots, I feel they enjoy great benefits under our legislation.
Would the minister allow me a question? What will happen to the pilots in the Cornwall-Montreal area?
I beg your pardon?
What will happen to the pilots in the Cornwall-Montreal district if, within a few years, all American ships can be piloted by Americans?

I am very pleased that my hon. friend has asked this question because as Minister of Transport, I was asked by the pilots themselves to grant compulsory pilotage in that district. In fact, in November 1960,
I told them: Your request is a serious one, and we shall do our utmost to grant it. After studying the matter, we imposed compulsory pilotage on all foreign ships. At the time, I indicated to the pilots that I was not prepared to impose compulsory pilotage on

American ships because we were then discussing pilotage on the great lakes. However, I asked the pilots to grant voluntary exemptions to American ships until the Canada Shipping Act was amended. Well, that is what happened, and the pilots themselves exempted American ships.
My hon. friend has asked what will happen to the pilots in that district. Well, their position is better today than it was in November 1960. We have improved their position. Moreover, I would point out to those who feel inclined to raise cries of persecution in a case like this, that I think there is a tendency to make a bogey out of everything that is done by the Department of Transport in regard to pilotage.
These pilots are members of an old association with traditions going back many years. They are jealous of their rights, and you may be sure I respect those rights. However, representations are constantly being made as if we wanted to deprive them of their livelihood. There is always a hue and cry whenever a word is changed in any document dealing with pilotage.
Pilots are now organized in a federation, they have well defined districts, their working hours have been reduced, their salaries and expense allowances have gone up from year to year. Considering that they were granted compulsory pilotage on all foreign vessels under the sole condition that American vessels be exempted, I feel that the pilots should not raise any bogey in such a case, because their situation has improved in that district since last November. It should be kept in mind especially that those districts did not even exist before. There was only the Ottawa-St. Lawrence district where pilotage was not compulsory. Consequently, they were at a disadvantage as compared with the pilots downstream from Montreal. Their position is much better nowadays. Pilotage has become compulsory. Their association is recognized and so are their districts. I think they have made a great step forward.
I know they did not get everything they wanted, but they have made a great step forward.
I feel that our agreement with the United States concerning the great lakes is both reasonable and justifiable. We did not twist their arm. We ensured fair treatment for our pilots. The United States agreed to our request, namely that there should be equal treatment right from the first year. They made

Canada Shipping Act
that concession and, in return, we made concessions on other points.
Consequently, I feel that as far as pilotage on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence is concerned, the pilots' situation is better now than it has ever been.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in the discussion on the third reading of this bill but I rise again because of the intervention by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) whom, I hope, will resume his seat. Incidentally, I also rise because of what the Minister of Transport just said.
First of all, with all respect, I say that the Minister of Transport added nothing to the debate a while ago. He only repeated what he had said yesterday. But he used a new phrase, that is, safety is the prime consideration.
The safety of the shipping traffic urges us to conclude an agreement with the United States. Very well. As a matter of fact, the pilots themselves have been saying that. That is why they asked the minister not to exempt from compulsory pilotage, as the minister says, from the payment of pilotage dues, United States ships. They claimed that if such an exemption is granted, what would surely happen, as the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) indicated, is that eventually there will be no more demand for Canadian pilots in that district. The United States ships will be handled through these dangerous waters by their own captains or masters, so that in five or ten years, there will be no need for Canadian pilots in that district.
Now the minister says that compulsory pilotage was granted the pilots. Prior to last November, no compulsory pilotage existed in that district.
Why was the pilotage made compulsory by the department in that district? For the same reason of course that brought the setting up of pilotage districts on the great lakes. It is on account of the increase in traffic in that area, because compared to the period which preceded the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, the volume of traffic has more than doubled. Ships are bigger and longer, with a deeper draught and a carrying capacity of 20,000 to 25,000 tons, which explains the need to ensure the safety of American, Canadian and foreign vessels in those waters by making pilotage compulsory.
Now, after having agreed to that in November, exemption is intended for American ships. Well, pilots are objecting to that.
There is no question of raising cries of persecution or of making a bogey out of that. Neither the hon. member for Levis, nor I ever said any such thing. We made our argument here the same way as the pilots did before the committee where I think, they very calmly made very logical representations. They feel it is an invasion of their rights and of our sovereignty over Canadian waters. Furthermore, they feel that safety of navigation is threatened and they put their case to the minister.
The minister says they are well treated and that their remuneration is excellent. Remuneration or salaries are not involved in that legislation; only two things are involved: upholding of sovereignty and protection against accidents.
(Text):
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Is it not a fact that even before November, 1960, when there were no compulsory requirements either as to dues or pilotage, all vessels using the seaway at that time employed pilots; and does the hon. member not think that in the future as in the past the safety of these valuable ships will be a factor whether or not pilots are employed, regardless of the legislative requirements?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think the answer to that question was given by the minister in committee, when he said that while it is true that most of the United States vessels are now using Canadian pilots because they are unfamiliar with the waters, there is no doubt that in due course the necessity of using Canadian pilots will gradually disappear and the day will come, which in our opinion is not far off, when the masters and mates on United States ships will be able, because of the experience they have gained, to take these ships right through to Montreal without using a Canadian pilot and therefore the pool of Canadian pilots will in due course disappear.
I wanted to say a word or two about some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Simcoe North. Since he understands so well what I am saying in French, perhaps I might continue in that language. However, it might not be courteous to do so. The hon. member concluded his remarks by asking whether the United States government would have spent upwards of $100 million without

Canada Shipping Act
having the assurance from Canada that they would obtain exemption from pilotage in this section of the river.

I think the hon. member misunderstood me. I said it was related to the problem of getting the United States government to spend $105 million in that particular section, and that part of the implied agreement must have been that we would approve canal facilities between St. Regis and Montreal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I took down the exact words that my hon. friend used, and I think they jibe very accurately with the argument he was trying to make. Why would the Americans spend over $100 million in the international section of the river if they did not expect to get the same treatment from Canada that the United States has given to Canada under the United States-Canada pilotage arrangement which he mentioned earlier?
The point is this, and it seems to have been forgotten entirely both by the hon. member and by the minister as well. We are dealing here with the international section and the international section alone. That is the point. It seems to have been forgotten both by the minister and the hon. member that in the international section, where the Americans have spent money for navigational facilities, they have all the protection that is required in so far as pilotage is concerned. They got it under the amendment to section VI of the pilotage act which was passed last year, and they also have it under their own legislation.
The point I am trying to make is that we are giving them in Canadian waters rights which they have not got today, rights which they have in United States waters under their own legislation and rights which they have in international waters by legislation which we passed last session. Now the hon. member comes forward and says we have received a quid pro quo, and that is why we have put this in the legislation. There may be a quid but I should like to know where the quo is. As the hon. member for Simcoe North has said, the quid is the exemption on lake Michigan. Canada gets rights for its Canadian pilots on that lake, which is wholly in United States territory. That is true. But why, and I have asked this question repeatedly, is that right of exemption on lake Michigan not placed in United States legislation in the same way that the right of exemption for United States ships is placed in Canadian legislation in this bill?
If it is a good thing to amend the Canada Shipping Act to give United States ships, because of certain commitments that have been made by Canada, the right to be exempt from pilotage in the Cornwall-Montreal
[Mr. Chevrier.l
district, why should the Americans not do the same thing in their legislation? The minister replied that their laws are not the same as ours. However, they have enacted certain laws so far as the great lakes pilotage area is concerned, and the question that comes to my mind is why should they not do it in this case?
The hon. member for Simcoe North attempted, and I say to him respectfully that he did not succeed, to argue away the treaty aspect of this matter. United States citizens were given rights in the international section of the river by treaties going back as far as 1783 and extending right up to the boundary waters treaty act of 1909. Those rights are clearly established in these treaties. It seems to me that if they are to have additional rights, particularly in the Canadian section of the river, it should be done by way of a treaty as well.
I know those who sit on the other side of the house challenge this argument, but it seems to me that there is a loss of sovereignty in these Canadian waters. It seems to me that the law so far as these Canadian waters from Montreal to Cornwall-St. Regis are concerned should remain as it was before, and I know the minister will reply at once that of course it does remain. It does not in this sense, that the pilots no longer have control in that section of the river, but they have in the section extending from Montreal to the sea. For that reason the pilots have come and protested against this legislation.
No one is challenging the statement that the pilots are well paid, but the pilots would not have been before the committee of the house as they were for two days protesting against this legislation unless they feared not only the international and safety aspects of it but also that it might represent a step toward taking from them certain rights in the river downstream. Furthermore, I am sure the pilots will continue their representations in that regard, which is indicative of the fact that they are not satisfied with this legislation.

Would the hon. member permit another question? I think the hon. gentleman is perhaps being deliberately obtuse. Does the hon. member think the United States in constructing the seaway would have spent $105 million, or whatever amount was spent, in the international section of the St. Lawrence if there had not been an undertaking, either firm or implied, on the part of the Canadian government to improve and deepen the canal between St. Regis and Montreal?

Americans made that expenditure without receiving that assurance. I am attempting to make that clear to the hon. gentleman but he will not let me reply. I wish to add this. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND RECOMMEND CHANGES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND RECOMMEND CHANGES
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to consider and recommend changes that may be desirable in the War Measures Act;
That the committee consist of fifteen members to be designated by the house;
That the committee be empowered to sit during the sittings of the house;
That the committee have power to send for persons and papers;
That the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as it may deem advisable and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation to the printing thereof; and
That the committee be empowered to report from time to time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, ever since 1914 there has been on the statute books of this country an act known as the War Measures Act, which

was passed immediately after the commencement of the first great war. Following that war there were discussions on various occasions both in the House of Commons and in the other place regarding this legislation, particularly as to whether or not it should continue in effect following the declaration of peace.
The act in question, and I shall make only a short reference to it, provides for the issue of a proclamation by Her Majesty, or under the authority of the governor in council, who may then "do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada"; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms-"the power to censor, control and suppress publications, writings, communications and means of communications, arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation, control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters, and the movement of vessels in Canada, and also the control of transportation by land, air or water, control of trade, exportation, importation, production and manufacture, as well as appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property". In other words, under the general powers there is virtually nothing that the governor in council cannot do within the powers granted by the act.
Following the second world war the government of Right Hon. Mackenzie King and later the government of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent brought in and had passed by parliament two acts which contained virtually the same powers as the War Measures Act, and enabled the governor in council to draft orders in council which, regardless of whether or not they were infringements on provincial jurisdiction, were none the less lawful.
In 1960 parliament passed the bill of rights and made certain provisions therein respecting some of the powers contained in the War Measures Act. Section 6 of the War Measures Act reads as follows:
The provisions of the three sections last preceding shall only be in force during war. invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended.
Those are the sections giving the power, imposing penalties, and providing that anyone held for deportation under this act, or under arrest and detention as an alien enemy, or upon suspicion of being an alien enemy, or to prevent his departure from Canada, shall be released upon bail or otherwise discharged or tried, without the consent of the Minister of Justice.

The bill of rights provides that section 6 of the War Measures Act is repealed and substitutes therefor the following:
Sections 3, 4 and 5 shall come into force only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists.
For the protection of the rights of parliament there is this provision. The proclamation declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue or, if parliament is not then sitting, within the first 15 days next thereafter. A further subsection provides that when the proclamation has been laid before parliament a notice of motion in either house signed by 10 members thereof, praying that the proclamation be revoked, shall be debated in that house at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the motion in the house is made. This section further provides that if both houses of parliament resolve that the proclamation be revoked, it shall cease to have effect. In other words there was restored to parliament the right to assure that the executive power exercised by the governor in council shall be subject to the elected representatives of the people.
Various hon. gentlemen participated in the debate on the bill of rights. I am not going to refer to what they said, but I would point out that their views are dealt with at length in Hansard of August 3, 1960, at page 7503, when clause 6 of the War Measures Act, as part of the bill of rights, was before the house. Various suggestions were made for amendments to the War Measures Act. At that time I said, as reported at page 7506:
If a committee is set up and, of course, I am in the hands of the house as always-
To which the hon. member for Essex East with his customary suavity remarked as follows:
The right hon. gentleman has some influence.
I said:
I thank my hon. friend for those kind words. His geniality has brought about the recognition of a fact that he often denies.
This would be a most important contribution to the Canada of today and to the Canada of the future. At that time we would not deal as we are asked to now on a piecemeal basis with the rights under the War Measures Act. If there is a degree of unanimity, and I think there will be, that Canadian citizens should not be deported the committee might make that recommendation along with such other recommendations as will bring about a war measures act which on the one hand will maintain the solidarity and security of the state and on the other hand will have before it the paramount necessity of not needlessly sacrificing the rights of Canadians.
Committee on War Measures Act
That summarizes the general tenor of the views expressed by me and also by the Minister of Justice. Later at page 7511 of Hansard I said:
In so far as this is concerned-
I was referring to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition.
-no naturalized Canadian may be deprived of his citizenship and no naturalized British subject may be deprived of his status as a British subject under this act, and we accept that as a desirable objective when full and complete amendment of the War Measures Act or other acts is made.
There seemed to be general agreement at that time that there was the necessity for parliament to have the opportunity to deal with this matter. It is not a partisan matter. I am not going into anything which by the greatest exaggeration could be considered as bringing partisan considerations into this debate. I simply say there was agreement that something should be done to bring about amendments to the War Measures Act and to assure that the act, while maintaining the need of security at all times, should be so altered or changed as to provide that security, while at the same time preserving to the greatest degree possible the rights of the individual.
On January 27, 1961, at page 1475 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition asked me this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he could confirm or deny a report in the press this morning to the effect that during this session the government is going to amend the War Measures Act?
I replied:
I did not see that report. The government feels -and it expressed its feeling in this regard at the time discussions were taking place relative to the bill of rights-that some committee of the house might well consider the War Measures Act and, having considered it, make recommendations as to what revisions or amendments could be made to that act to render it a measure from which injustice would not follow.
A little later on I said:
I feel and I think the Leader of the Opposition will agree, that a full and complete review of the War Measures Act would be following a course in keeping with the desires of Canadians as a whole. In time of war the measure is necessary in the interests of maintaining security, but in the days of peace there cannot be too large a degree of justification for its maintenance in effect without giving parliament at least the opportunity, through a committee, of fully considering the representations that have been made from time to time with regard to this legislation.
Following that, the hon. member for Essex East indicated that a private member had a bill on the order paper showing the intention to introduce amendments to the War Measures Act. With customary modesty he did not refer to himself but simply said an hon. member had such a bill on the order paper. Later, on

Committee on War Measures Act May 29, the Leader of the Opposition asked this question as recorded at page 5504 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister, having regard to the statements made by him during the debate last year on the bill of rights and similar statements on January 27 this year, whether the government intends to submit the War Measures Act to this session of parliament for consideration?
To which I replied:
I can only say at this time that depending on the progress that is made in the house, a decision in that regard will be announced to the house.
Again a supplementary question was asked by the hon. member for Essex East. All this indicates, I think, that there is a desire to bring about a close scrutiny and examination of this legislation. I had hoped to bring it before the house yesterday, but in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition and at the request of the hon. member for Laurier the motion was set over until today.
