speechtext:
I hope the house will accept this motion. I realize that many hon. members will argue, as they have argued throughout the session, that committees are becoming too numerous. This committee is one on which I am sure all who are chosen will be most happy and honoured to serve. It is the kind of constructive work in which members who wish to devote themselves to the maintenance of our freedoms will naturally desire to take part.
The question might arise as to how long this committee would sit. I think a start should be made. Many representations were made in 1960 and prior thereto. Various groups of lawyers, constitutional law professors and professors of history made representations. Professor Lower, professor emeritus of Queen's, has given many years of study to this question. I think of others equally well in-tentioned and well equipped who would be most desirous of playing their parts in this investigation and examination, and also in making recommendations consonant with the purpose of the legislation, but at the same time assuring the preservation of those things that should not be denied to Canadians.
This is now the 13th of June. I have no idea how long the session will continue, but the progress that has been made would seem to lend support to the hope that by the end of this month we should be in a position to conclude. If, however, we are not, I want the house to make its own determination. In that regard I return to a view that I expressed earlier, that in the interests of hon. members, particularly those with families including


small children, they should not be denied the opportunity to be with their families during the months of July and August.
During the summer the committee might conceivably exchange ideas and views on this particular matter and have representations made while not necessarily having to convene. In that way the committee would perform its duty without inconvenience or interfering with the legitimate desires of members not only to do that to which I have already referred, but also to see their constituents. Therefore, without further argument, I place this motion before the house. It may be contended it should have been done earlier. That will always be an argument; but if it had been done there would have been one more committee in addition to the number already sitting, about which complaint has been made.
Is this a necessary work to be done? I think it is. I do not feel that recommendations for amendment of this legislation should be the prerogative of departmental officials or cabinet ministers. This legislation crosses all party lines, and members of the committee when chosen will be able to do something to meet the anomalous situation which has prevailed in two world wars and following, that while we fought for freedom we found it necessary to place in bond as security for their preservation, the freedoms for which we fought.
I hope the house will accept this motion so the committee may commence the discharge of its duties and make decisions as to such suggestion as I made earlier, so as to enable not only the exchange of ideas between members of the committee, but also the reception of ideas from those learned in the law and also those learned in the processes of freedom. Then, the committee may bring about recommendations which will maintain the essence of the War Measures Act as the instrument for the mobilization of our people should war ever come and at the same time preserve so far as possible those things which are dearer than life itself.

And to the extent indicated in the bill of rights itself, to which I will make reference in a moment. The Prime Minister has suggested that because of the importance of this measure and the common attitude that prevails about considering amendments, this is not in itself the kind of question that should divide the house. I readily agree that such is the case. The Prime Minister will not expect me, of course, to refrain from putting on the record with regard to this matter which seem desirable in the light of the position we took last session with regard to amendments to the War Measures Act. However, with his general statement I do not quarrel.
The Prime Minister will recall, as he himself has reminded us by his several references to Hansard, that questions were put to the government and in particular to the Prime Minister asking when steps would be taken to bring about amendments to the War Measures Act. The Prime Minister mentioned one of the replies he made in which he said by way of response, I think somewhat vaguely, that it would depend largely on the progress that was made during the course of the present session.
I take the position, of course, that this is not the view the Prime Minister took when we discussed this matter in 1960. I believe his words in that regard, to which I will refer later, were more definitive than was the indication given in reply to the questions put to him during the course of this session by the Leader of the Opposition.
The Prime Minister has referred to the fact that there is now on the order paper a bill standing in my name which embodies the proposed amendments to the War Measures Act which were submitted last session in this house by the Leader of the Opposition and later in the committee on the bill of rights, by me, supported by the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve-Rosemont.
The practical consideration, however, is one that we must bear in mind. The government brings in, on the 13th day of June, a proposal that a committee should be established for the purpose of considering the War Measures Act and any amendments thereto. Under our procedures a bill introduced by the

Committee on War Measures Act government, of course, will likely have precedence over a bill proposed by a private member of this house. If it is a fact that my bill, which obviously encouraged the government at long last to take some action, is to be superseded by the action taken today by the government, then of course I can have no legitimate procedural complaint, nor would any such complaint get very far. I would be practical enough to recognize that situation at once.
That being the case, and if this is the government's final stand in the matter, as one who wants to see amendments to the War Measures Act and who wants to see the War Measures Act brought into a position consistent with the bill of rights I would under those conditions, of course, support the motion proposed today by the Prime Minister. However, I would do that not without some complaint on other grounds.
It is regrettable that this particular motion was not presented early in the session. We have complained from time to time that the government's mismanagement of the business of this house has been such as to crowd in, in the dying days of the session, not only much important legislation to be considered exclusively in this chamber, and other legislation to be considered by parliamentary committees, but as well the work of many of the standing and special committees of this house, with the result that not only are we sitting from 11 o'clock in the morning until 10.30 o'clock at night in the House of Commons but at the same time we have obligations in committees that are meeting simultaneously, some three times, some four times and on one occasion five times in a day, with one committee actually having had its sittings-I refer to the external affairs committee which is an extremely important one-during the luncheon recess from one o'clock until two thirty in the afternoon.
With the background of this heavy schedule for our committee and house work, the government now comes forward at this late moment to present this motion, which could well have been presented in the month of January. If it had been presented at that time, ample opportunity this session would have been provided for consultation with law experts and other competent people outside to assist in our deliberations of the amendments thought desirable in the War Measures Act.
The Prime Minister will therefore not be surprised if, seeking to be as conciliatory as possible at this time of the session, I lay before him with some justification our complaint for not having brought this measure forward early in the session. That was the time to bring forward something about which the government had been properly forewarned and

which indeed the Prime Minister himself, as he indicated in what he said today, had suggested to the house would be the action taken by the government during the course of the present session. I believe this matter is so important that we ought to begin the work of this committee at once, if that is to be the procedural situation in relation to the bill now standing in my name.
The Prime Minister has referred to some observations of Professor Lower. I am not surprised that he should do so, because Professor Lower obviously is a protagonist of the Prime Minister. He made that fact clear in the committee on the bill of rights when he spoke glowingly of the Prime Minister's efforts and generally of certain other points of view and positions taken by the Prime Minister.
I do not fail to recognize the merits of Professor Lower, although I would not be as enthusiastic, and the Prime Minister would not expect me to be-

I am going to quote him. I would not be as enthusiastic nor would the Prime Minister expect me to be as enthusiastic about him as within this limited context Professor Lower has been of the Prime Minister. However, Professor Lower made this statement, and I refer to page 5650 of Hansard of July 1, 1960, and to words quoted by the Leader of the Opposition:
I submit that if we are going to have a bill of rights in Canada, and there will be a great deal of debate about it, we ought to have one that means something. I believe that in normal peacetime our liberties are not in very serious danger. But in wartime they are in very serious danger, the liberties of all of us. Hence, it is the duty of the government to find a method of enacting legislation which will give at least minimum guarantees. Suggestions could be made which would modify the War Measures Act. In the meantime, as long as it is on the books it is the duty of everybody who loves a free society, who loves liberty, to bend his best efforts to attack this act and try to get rid of this invidious liberty-destroying statute, the War Measures Act.
I do not agree, and I am sure the Prime Minister does not agree, with this full denunciation of the War Measures Act, because I think we feel that human liberty already recognizes that in wartime there are certain exigencies in the interests of the security of the state which must be borne in mind. Professor Lower has expressed his views in a number of other publications. In the Canadian Commentator of March, 1959, he wrote an article entitled "The Bill of Rights" in which he said:
The Canadian War Measures Act is the most iniquitous piece of legislation ever to disgrace a British statute book-at least since the celebrated legislation-by-proclamations act of Henry VIII, 400 years ago. Its parallel is to be found not in any

other English-speaking country, for none have disgraced themselves in this respect as has Canada done-*
Then he went on to say:
If Mr. Diefenbaker, in the fullness of his wisdom, decided tomorrow that a state of apprehended insurrection existed, and proclaimed the War Measures Act, he could call parliament and the immense liberty-loving Conservative majority behind him, shocked at his conduct, might then proceed by open vote in the commons, to require him to withdraw his proclamation. This provision (section 6, etc.) is fantastic in its futility. I cannot understand how serious-minded public men can have the effrontery to put such words on paper. And yet there they are. If Mr. Diefenbaker has any regard to his future reputation-
I suspect that the Prime Minister has, and that would be understandable:
- (especially among those who make or mar the reputations of public men, that is, the historians and the constitutionalists), he will withdraw this section of his bill.
So the Prime Minister is right-

speechtext:
Yes. So the Prime Minister is right in saying that Professor Lower had strong views about the War Measures Act, particularly in relation to the bill of rights. It is a fact that in the committee on the bill of rights I asked Professor Lower whether in view of his strongly expressed views regarding the War Measures Act he did not think appropriate amendments should be made to that act in the bill of rights. He answered in the affirmative. I think I should point out, in fairness, that after I left the room the Minister of Justice -and this is a matter of record in Hansard; the minister was not taking advantage of my absence and it was a mere coincidence; I mean that sincerely-put questions to Professor Lower and as a result got from him replies in direct contradiction to the position he had taken earlier in the committee.
This does not in any way affect the merits of the proposal now before the house, but since Professor Lower's name was mentioned I thought I should let the Prime Minister know that I was not unaware that this great admirer of his had strong views on this matter, views which in principle if not in every detail coincide with those expressed by the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke in this house on the occasion of the second reading of the bill of rights. On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition pointed out that the only change made in the bill of rights regarding the War Measures Act was to make possible parliamentary debate on the proclamation of the War Measures Act, which of course brings that act into force, and on its revocation. The bill of 90205-6-395J
13. 1961
Committee on War Measures Act rights provides that after such debate parliament may take a particular course of action as to whether or not it wishes to withdraw the proclamation. The point is that there was reference in the bill of rights to the War Measures Act, but only within the limited terms I have just mentioned.
The Leader of the Opposition urged that there should be amendments to the War Measures Act, and that these amendments should be incorporated in the bill of rights. While he recognized that the mere reference to the War Measures Act in section 5 of the bill of rights represented an improvement, he argued that it did not go far enough. The Leader of the Opposition said that because of the way the bill of rights dealt with the War Measures Act we were giving to the latter a greater sanctity and a greater prestige than was necessary or desirable, and that we were giving it as well a pre-eminence by that kind of amendment, rather than dealing with it in its form.
The Leader of the Opposition also pointed out that notwithstanding this provision in the bill of rights the law would remain in such a position that whatever had been done before would continue to be possible, notwithstanding the passage of the bill of rights. But he did point out-I think this is important for us to note, and it is something that Professor Lower has not taken into consideration-that we have to take into account war emergencies and, while that is the case, he would be a bold man who would argue that war emergencies may not make it necessary in the future for persons to be detained in a manner that apart from the exigencies of war would seem undesirable, not because of any act they had done but because of the danger of what they might do with regard to certain acts which obviously would involve the security of the state.
The War Measures Act, as the Prime Minister said, was placed on the statute books in 1914. As the Prime Minister said, it gives to the governor in council, in time of war, virtually unlimited powers to restrain the freedom of the person of the Canadian citizen. The Prime Minister did not note, however, that since the passage of the act we have adopted in our own Canadian Citizenship Act legislation that now makes it impossible for the government in peacetime to deprive any Canadian citizen, resident in Canada, of his citizenship.
Notwithstanding that, the Leader of the Opposition urged that we should now go a step forward. He said that any bill of rights should contain a provision limiting the powers given to the governor in council under the War Measures Act by expressly excluding from those powers the power by order in

Committee on War Measures Act council to deprive any Canadian citizen of his citizenship. The Leader of the Opposition argued, and I believe we would all agree with this, that the governor in council should be expressly forbidden to act under the War Measures Act to banish or exile any citizen from our country. I think we would wish it were possible to agree that the governor in council should be expressly forbidden, even in wartime, to detain any citizen or resident of our country without providing for an early trial on charges specifically laid in accordance with the law of Canada.
However, I am sure careful reflection will suggest that this would not be a responsible thing for parliament to do, and we are not prepared to go that far. Certainly in the bill I have before this house we do not take that extreme position. Nevertheless we in this party do feel that there should be, in the light of all that has transpired, a limitation by law on the absolute and arbitrary power of the governor in council to detain persons, even in wartime. We believe that a provision should have been written into the bill of rights which would limit the power of the governor in council to detain any person for more than let us say three months, or the period might be less, without a hearing before a supreme court judge and satisfying that judge that there were serious grounds for believing that the detention of such person was essential to the security of the state.
This measure, in so far as the Prime Minister is concerned, admittedly has a long association. I remind the Prime Minister that it was on May 16, 1947, when he as a private member of this house recommended not only that there should be amendments to the War Measures Act but as well that the Official Secrets Act should be repealed. The latter act was objectionable, I suppose, on the ground that it presumed guilt on the part of an accused contrary to the common law tradition which has existed for a long time and contrary to section 3(f) of the bill of rights, which now guarantees by law that an accused person is presumed to be innocent until proven otherwise.
The Prime Minister said in 1960 when this matter was discussed, as may be found on page 5948 of Hansard for July 7 of that year:
I think the whole act-
He was referring, of course, to the War Measures Act.
-deserves to be considered... I think if we could get together the membership in the house and deal with the War Measures Act and ascertain the degree to which the rights of the individual may be maintained to the highest extent without detriment to the security of the nation as a whole, changes and amendments might be made to that act. If hon. members of the house so desire, I would be willing that at the next session a committee

be set up to consider this whole field, for the War Measures Act, like all measures passed for the purpose of ensuring the salvation and survival of the state, has been found in the light of experience not only here but in other countries to contain provisions that ought to be ameliorated or subdued in the interests of the individual while at the same time maintaining the security of the state.
The Prime Minister referred to some parts of this discussion, but I did not note that he read all that was relevant. I may be wrong in that particular. I formed the impression, listening to the recital of what he did say in 1960, that he did not give the full text as I find it before me now in volume 6 of Hansard for last session. I had been urging, as indeed, had the Leader of the Opposition, that we should incorporate into the bill of rights certain amendments which we proposed. By such incorporation, we would bring the War Measures Act, without depriving it of its desired strength, into a form consistent with the bill of rights.

In my judgment, to have waited all this time demonstrates that the government was not as concerned about those amendments as it professes to be. It would not have been difficult for the government to come forward with this proposal early in the session when we could have given the matter the fullest consideration. However, it has chosen another course. It has chosen to increase our work in the dying days of the session in such a manner as to make it impossible for every member to give full consideration to the work of the house. There is not a member within sound of my voice who does not know that what I am saying is true. That is the situation. The country knows it. The country must know the kind of pressure that has been put upon us in the dying days of the session in the effort to discharge our duties.
However, the government has finally brought forward this measure. I hope the committee will be set up forthwith. Committee on War Measures Act because of being detained I missed the usual demonstration of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) laconism in introducing questions of this kind, his usual gems of language and his explanation of the legalities surrounding a problem of this nature. However, shortly after my arrival I was briefed by a fellow member as to what the Prime Minister had said so I think I have a very good idea of his remarks in introducing this motion.
I think everyone will realize that as a layman I suffer some disadvantage in following such legal luminaries as the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who are well versed in legal problems and constitutional matters. However, regardless of that I wish to assure the house that although I am a sort of simple, naive layman I have always had a great interest in this question and I fully realize and appreciate the purpose and the importance of this motion. While I am not able to discourse on the legal aspects of the question with any degree of knowledge compared with the previous speakers, I can say that I am one who always has been easily aroused by injustices and any transgression of human rights and human dignity has always concerned me.
In fact, over the years and until recent years I felt almost frustrated and exasperated on occasions at the lack of understanding of other persons' rights and I felt at times that I was tilting against windmills. I will say that I feel the situation in Canada has changed quite rapidly in recent years. More and more people are realizing what the citizen's rights are in a democratic state.
Like the previous speaker, I regret that this very important motion has been introduced at this late date in the session. The question is an important and serious one that requires time for almost leisurely study, shall I say. It is not one of those technical questions where you can deal with the matter with exactitude after certain facts have been produced. There is an infinite variety of aspects to a problem of this nature. Plenty of time must be taken for the hearing of views of legal authorities by the committee, for hearing the views of representatives of various sections of the community throughout the land and even the views of individuals who have paid a great deal of attention to this subject and have studied it for many years. Following the hearing of these views, I am sure the committee will require some time before it arrives at its conclusion.
This is a subject that will arouse a great deal of interest. As I said before, even in the smaller places I find that in recent years there is more interest in this topic than there was years ago. Years ago it was considered too

abstract, not in the ordinary day's activities, shall I say, but there is greater concern and interest now and the committee will need plenty of time to give consideration to the evidence, facts, views, suggestions and recommendations presented to it. Members of the house as individuals will want time to read the evidence and proceedings of the committee and I believe plenty of time should be provided. Later when legislation is introduced the house will want ample time to discuss this very important question properly and at suitable length. On that account I say again that we in this group regret that this motion was not introduced earlier in the session.
I am not going into the legal aspects of the matter. I am only going to deal with it from a broad point of view. As I said before, I am not competent to deal with the niceties of such a problem but I can deal with its impact on the citizen and speak of it in general terms. I believe that several advantages can flow from the passage of this motion, the study of the problem by the committee, by members of the house generally and the consequent proposed amendments to the War Measures Act. First of all, I think that the primary advantage is that the legislation will make certain, as far as it is humanly possible to do so under the circumstances, that the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens are protected in periods of emergency. I think that is the primary advantage.
Then I think there are two or three others. I believe that the gathering of evidence, facts, opinions, suggestions and recommendations from all those sectors of the Canadian community should prove of value to the present generation and to future generations. The record itself should prove of great value. Then I believe that the hearings of the committee and the discussion of the problem generally in the house and in the country will provide general interest in the subject and I am sure, as the result of happenings in recent years-[DOT] I am talking of happenings within the last ten or fifteen years, particularly since the second world war-greater understanding will be brought about. If the committee fulfils its responsibility and if the government accepts those recommendations which will come from people in all groups of society with various political opinions, including persons who support the group for which I have the honour to speak at the present time. I believe this whole study and consequent legislation will do something more to strengthen the sinews of democracy.
The average citizen is not learned in the law and is not learned in parliamentary procedure but he is interested in the basic rights of the citizen in a democracy. When you find

that this average citizen has a greater understanding, democracy is strengthened to that extent. We must realize that. While we are complacent and while we have accepted without question our freedom and our rights throughout the years, when we view the world around us it is marvellous to note how, under certain circumstances and certain emergency conditions, those rights can crumble if they are not supported by an informed citizenry.
In conclusion I wish to say that this group will co-operate in the work of the committee and in making suggestions as to amendments to the War Measures Act and will do all it can to the end that the demands of freedom and the rights of Canadian citizens are better served by this resolution, the consequent legislation and the action of this parliament. Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss this motion of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister
13, 1361
Committee on War Measures Act (Mr. Diefenbaker), which is one more evidence of the right hon. gentleman's real interest and determination to protect the rights and freedoms of the citizens of this country. It is one more step in the steady progress which has been made since the right hon. gentleman assumed the office of Prime Minister to undo the steady erosion of our rights and liberties which had taken place over the previous 22 years.
In discussing matters of this sort it is generally desirable to be calm and not to introduce notes of criticism. Of course, when dealing with intemperate speeches such as that of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) one recognizes that the hon. member gets carried away with a sense of his oratory, if not importance, and makes allowance for this kind of speech on that account. However, the hon. member did say something which I think calls for comment, because if there were no comment it would stand unanswered on the record of Hansard.
The first thing I wish to say simply by way of reply to my hon. friend is that he shows now a refreshing change of attitude from that which he showed during the many years he was a member of the treasury benches. Indeed, the government of which he was a part had 22 years in office during which time they had ample opportunity to deal with the War Measures Act and to remove from it those features which constitute the possibility, if not the fact, of an undue interference with human rights and fundamental freedoms. It was conspicuous then, and it is more conspicuous now in view of the hon. member's present attitude, that the previous administration did nothing during that time to bring about the results which the hon. member now professes himself so anxious to achieve.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when we listened this afternoon to the strictures heaped upon the government for not getting on with this proposal sooner, I think we are able to put the hon. gentleman's strictures in their proper perspective by recalling that his conversion, although we may welcome it, is very late.
The hon. member cannot take refuge in the answer that this measure is only necessary now because we did not have a bill of rights before; therefore his party and his government were blameless, because they did not have a bill of rights and it is the bill of rights that makes this necessary. It will be recalled that in the discussion of the bill of rights itself last year during all that lengthy period when we had to listen to the strictures he heaped upon that measure, he persisted in saying it added nothing by way of rights but was a mere codification of existing rights. If that is the hon. member's view, then the

Committee on War Measures Act rights which are in the bill of rights now existed at the time the hon. gentleman held office and the War Measures Act was as much in conflict with those rights then as it is now.
The hon. gentleman is now so anxious to see something done that he professes to claim exclusive credit for everything that is being done, yet, as I say, in all those years he was unable to see the importance of the measure which the Prime Minister has now brought forward. It is well understood, of course, that there is no one so keen as a recent convert and we welcome the hon. member to the ranks of the converted, the ranks of those who are now prepared to align themselves in support of the liberty of the individual. In contrast to the sudden conversion and the over eagerness now displayed by the hon. gentleman, may I emphasize that this government has been proceeding steadily and surely to the restoration and protection of those rights which were so eroded in earlier years. A major step was the enactment of the biU of rights itself. At that time the Prime Minister gave an undertaking that he would look at the War Measures Act and invite parliament to consider in what ways it might be amended so as to bring it into harmony with the bill of rights, and do what could be done to protect the rights of citizens even in times of emergency without unduly prejudicing the interests of the state as a whole.
Pursuant to the bill of rights we have brought in two important amendments to statutes this year to bring them into line with the bill of rights, and now comes this further measure initiated by the Prime Minister in order to make amends for the 22 years of erosion of rights-the motion we are now debating to set up a committee to examine the War Measures Act. Indeed, when one considers the change of attitude of the hon. member for Essex East I cannot help, while listening to him, thinking that he displays all the frustrated inconsistency which would be displayed by the outcome of a cross between a leopard and a chameleon, because you know, Mr. Speaker, the leopard's trouble is that he cannot change his spots while the chameleon changes colour with every perch upon which he alights. We come now to consider this motion which the hon. member professed a desire to see carried because that would have the result of amendments being made to the War Measures Act, and yet the hon. member has invited you, Mr. Speaker, to rule this motion out of order. Of course, with your usual wisdom and perspicacity you refused to entertain the point of order which the hon. member sought to raise, but the extraordinary thing to contemplate is this measure of frustration felt


by the hon. member for Essex East. He is so frustrated because he cannot himself claim the exclusive credit for what is being done that he forgets he has told us he intends to support the measure and solemnly invites Your Honour to rule it out of order. I think all members will understand the situation and accept the speech made by the hon. gentleman with the caution and reserve which it deserves.
What, then, of the proposal of the Prime Minister which is now before us, a proposal consistent with the undertaking which he gave last year when we were considering the bill of rights? This proposal, I suggest, sets out the proper way of dealing with this problem. The opposition has consistently suggested that we should get the bill of rights and the War Measures Act all mixed up and confused. Indeed, this desire on their part to confuse things was brought to my mind by one of the comments made by the hon. member for Essex East when he said the government had the habit of putting certain problems into one basket and certain other problems in another basket. He seemed to think this was a matter for criticism. It seems to me that this orderly method of dealing with things is the proper method instead of getting them all mixed up until, like the hon. member for Essex East, they are hopelessly confused. We have persistently and consistently taken the position that these matters should be dealt with separately because that is the most effective method of dealing with them.
When the bill of rights was before the special committee of the house last year there was a lengthy discussion on the bill in context with the War Measures Act and, as has been pointed out, one of the chief witnesses in this regard was Professor Lower of Queen's University. Professor Lower certainly repeated then a stricture he had uttered earlier against the War Measures Act and urged strongly on the committee that parliament should repeal the War Measures Act. It is true that Professor Lower at one point in his evidence did comment on the fact that we had incorporated in the bill of rights itself the provision having the effect that if the government proclaimed the War Measures Act due to a state of emergency parliament would have the right to review that proclamation and if it felt that the state of emergency was imaginary rather than real it would have the right to overrule the proclamation. Professor Lower did at one stage say this was a meaningless provision, particularly when he was being prompted in that regard by the hon. member for Essex East. also significant to note that Professor Lower admitted the necessity for some legislation conferring special powers on the government in time of war. I refer to his evidence at page 321 of the committee reports when he was being questioned by the hon. member for Essex East. The passage reads as follows:

speechtext:
Yes.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think we can properly and with justification say we can call to witness, as supporting our present action, one of the foremost opponents or critics of the War Measures Act in its present form, who stated clearly before the special committee of the House of Commons last year that he thought the sensible thing to do, as we did by the bill of rights, was to enact a bill of rights standing on its own feet, putting in safeguards immediately against a fictitious declaration of emergency which would give the government an opportunity to abuse the emergency powers, and then to make a lengthy and full study of the War Measures Act itself to see what changes to the measure should be made to bring it into conformity with the spirit of the bill of rights.
It is in that spirit that we have been studying this problem in the interim. As I said in the committee, which comment is contained in the portion I just quoted, and with which Professor Lower agreed, when we get into the realm of the War Measures Act we are getting into the realm of very difficult philosophical as well as legal problems. That is the area and the extent to which it is justifiable to ask parliament itself to give to the government, in times of real emergency, powers which, under normal circumstances, the government should not only not use, but


should not even possess, because they are definitely contrary to the kind of situation which prevails in normal time of peace.
The extent to which the War Measures Act could go, and should go, is the problem which we have been considering during all this intervening period because, unlike the hon. member for Essex East, we have the responsibility of ensuring that the government will in time of war-which we hope to God will never come-have the ample powers which it needs to safeguard the interests of the state. Simultaneously we have the responsibility of ensuring that the powers given to the government do not go further than those which are necessary for that purpose.
One must be very careful, as I am sure every hon. member will realize, as to what one does, because two things must be remembered. The kind of war that would confront us in these days is such that events will move with such swiftness there will not be time to commence changing legislation then, nor to determine the limits of powers. If one gets oneself into that situation, it may well be, and indeed probably will be, too late to ask parliament to extend the powers. Therefore, one has to be conscious of the fact that too severe limitations on the powers of government in time of real emergency would be in the long run perhaps more dangerous than a rather restricted recognition of the rights and liberties of the individual.
It is hard to crystallize this matter in a few words, but this is the sort of problem that we have had in mind in approaching the War Measures Act in the context of the bill of rights. That is one of the reasons why we were not able, as readily and as rapidly as my hon. friend from Essex East thought desirable, to produce a concrete proposal to lay before this house. The hon. member for Essex East made the extraordinary and, indeed, absurd suggestion that it was his bill, introduced in January, which had the result of causing the Prime Minister to introduce this proposal now in June. If we were as frightened of the results of the hon. member's efforts as he seems to suggest, I hardly think that would be consistent with the position that he has taken, nor that we should have waited from January to June before proceeding as we now are. The fact of the matter is that the main reason this proposal comes forward at this time is because the government is now in the position to meet with members of parliament and to discuss with them the changes which should be made or considered to be appropriate in the War Measures Act.
The Prime Minister has outlined how this committee might proceed. I would ask the liberty of perhaps elaborating a little on what

he said, to the following effect. It is true that this motion comes in late in the session, on June 13, at a time when it may be difficult to arrange in the immediate future for an opportunity for the widespread hearing of members of the public which will undoubtedly be desired. I suggest that one useful method by which the committee itself might consider the matter-and of course the committee will be master of its own proceedings and will determine for itself how it should proceed-might be as follows. When the committee first meets the government might, through those persons who have the responsibility for advising in these matters, present an outline to the committee for the committee's information of the sort of problem that arises in times of emergency represented by war.
I think it will be helpful to the committee to have that outline as a sort of indication of the scope of the problem with which we are dealing. Then the government would be prepared to lay before the committee a draft bill for its consideration. That bill would not be in the form of a "take it or leave it" document, but in the form of a specific draft in order that the committee may have something concrete before it. Then the committee might consider that, after some preliminary study, the matter could stand over for a while, during which time the draft bill could be circulated to all those individuals and organizations who would be interested in commenting on it. It might well be, therefore, that during the summer months this process could be going on and whenever parliament comes together again the committee would be in a position to continue its study and to hear the views of those to whom in the meantime the draft would have been circulated.
I put this forward as one suggested method of procedure only which the committee might consider. It might prefer to consider others, or it may prefer others, but it does seem to me this could be a very logical method of proceeding, and it was with this in mind that the Prime Minister made his suggestion earlier today, and it was with this thought in mind that we felt that this would be an appropriate time to bring this resolution before the house. That is all there was to it, and we had not any of the evil motives in mind attributed to us by the hon. member for Essex East.
Perhaps I should just conclude with a reference to some of the things that it might be suggested should be accomplished by any amendments to the War Measures Act. Some of these may have crossed the minds of my hon. friends opposite or some of them. If so,
Committee on War Measures Act this is all to the good. This problem of amendments to the War Measures Act is not a problem of any one party or another in this house; it is a problem for the House of Commons, the parliament of Canada and the Canadian nation.
The War Measures Act is not the interest or the property of any one party. It is the means by which or through which in times of war a government will be entrusted with the necessary powers for the effective and successful prosecution of that war. And if, therefore, there are views held in common here as to the lengths to which we can go and the limits to be put on the lengths to which we should go in amending the War Measures Act, it is all to the good. It does seem to me these are some of the areas in which it might be thought appropriate to amend the War Measures Act.
First, amendments placing limits upon the rights of the governor in council to authorize the deportation of Canadian citizens. Second, it may well be considered whether or not we should amend the War Measures Act to take away the power to deprive Canadian citizens of their citizenship under the War Measures Act without in any way interfering with any other statute, the citizenship act itself, which confers those powers. Therefore we certainly may well consider whether it is not perfectly proper and indeed essential to limit the power to take away citizenship under an emergency measures act such as the War Measures Act.
Again, we might consider the question of whether persons detained under the emergency powers of the War Measures Act should have the right of hearing written into the act itself. I would think hon. members would feel that such a hearing should not be held in open court before the ordinary judicial tribunal. Professor Lower and I exchanged some views and the hon. member for Essex East and Professor Lower exchanged some views on this in the committee last year; but it certainly might be considered whether there might not be provided in the statute itself some right of review of the detentions under these emergency powers.
Then there are several sections of the War Measures Act, it seems to me, such as sections 5, 8 and 9, which could well be looked at to see whether they are really necessary at all. The committee could consider whether they should be repealed or amended so that if continued they are left over in substantially modified form. As I have indicated the government-

Mr. Chairman, I think the discussion will be relatively short in connection with the schedule and therefore perhaps it is not necessary to consider it point by point.
My remarks are concerned with paragraph 22 of the schedule. That paragraph gives to this corporation a monopoly in the operation of this bridge over any other bridge, tunnel or ferry service, save only the ferry operated at the present time by the city of Three Rivers, for a radius of 25 miles above and 25 miles below the site of the bridge.
I assume this means that within a total distance of 50 miles no other person can build or operate a bridge, tunnel or ferry over or under the St. Lawrence river during the period of eight years from the sanction of this bill. I do not know whether that means eight years from February 2, 1956, or eight years from the passage of the bill now before us. In any event, it is not only covered for a period of eight years, which I presume is the construction period, but it is also covered for the whole period of the utilization of the proposed bridge. So long as the bridge

is in use, no other person can build any bridge, ferry or tunnel within a 50 mile area of the site of the bridge; that is, an area of 25 miles each side of the bridge.
It seems to me this is a rather unusual degree of power and authority and an unusual amount of monopoly to give to a corporation.
I presume that initially it was done to cover the period of time until the indebtedness of the bridge was paid off by way of tolls collected. If this was the intention, I think it should be so stated in the bill. Perhaps one could accept that sort of proposal in the light of whatever circumstances might be applicable. However, I think it is an extremely unique power to give forever, to the corporation, or so long as the bridge is utilized. The corporation is in a monopoly position in this regard and no other person is allowed to build a bridge, ferry or tunnel in this area.
It may well be that the growth of this part of the province of Quebec which will be served by the bridge will make it inadequate in a few years' time to serve the traffic that uses it. This is quite apart from the discussion we had earlier about the width of the bridge and why it could not be built in such a way that would allow expansion for additional lanes of traffic. This monopoly provision is even more difficult to appreciate.
I certainly would not wish this committee to take this action and then within a period of ten or 15 years find the bridge totally inadequate to serve the area, in view of the traffic using it. We would not want to prevent the legislature of the province of Quebec from having additional bridges constructed as time goes on.

Not too many years after the bridge was constructed it was found to be completely inadequate to handle the traffic using it. Within five or six years of this bridge being constructed by a private company it was purchased by the tolls, bridges and highway authority of the provincial government, and the provincial government subsequently built another bridge a few miles from the first one in order to deal with the volume of traffic travelling between the north Vancouver area and the lower mainland part of the city of Vancouver.

I beg to disagree here with the previous speaker who said this bill was actually setting up a monopoly.
It is too bad the hon. member has not yet had the opportunity of visiting that beautiful district of the province of Quebec. He would have discovered that topographically the site is not at all suited for the erection of another bridge, first of all because of the width of the river, and second, because of the difficulties of approach on the south and north shores in all other locations.
The nearest large commercial centre is located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river at Sorel. A bridge construction in that location would raise difficulties which could be overcome only with a considerable capital outlay.
Furthermore, when the provincial legislature examined the request submitted by "La Corporation du Pont de Trois-Rivieres", it unanimously granted the request. Exclusive rights were granted the corporation, not to create a monopoly but to insure that the project would be seriously dealt with.
The amount of $35,000 has already been spent for the preparation of plans, and that amount was raised through voluntary contributions raised in the Three Rivers area.
The drive was conducted long before the passing of the bill incorporating "La Corporation du Pont de Trois-Rivieres" by the provincial legislature.
If we are today faced with the situation that the corporation has to submit its case to parliament, it is because the governor in council cannot on his own authority grant permission for the erection of a bridge over the St. Lawrence seaway.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps, because of the importance of this bill, I should make a few brief comments. I shall attempt to be brief because I realize some hon. members on the other side of the house intend to make some comments.
Bill No. S-16 proposes an act to incorporate a public company under the name of National Mortgage Corporation of Canada. This company is being formed because of an apparent need for secondary mortgage financing. This need was set out in an article entitled "An Investment Opportunity" written by J. L. Whitney, one of the incorporating directors, in the Financial Post on August 1, 1959. Shortly after that a group of interested individuals began to study all of the problems. As a result of this study and negotiation this company now requests incorporation.
The bill has a threefold purpose. One, that the company be allowed to deal in mortgages. Two, that the company be given the power to raise funds for investment in N.H.A. and conventional mortgages, through the sale of mortgage bonds to investors. Third, to give the company the power to carry on the business of managing and servicing mortgages, not only those which are owned by its policyholders, but also those which are owned by other individuals and corporations and which are left with the company for the purpose of being serviced.
It is the hope of the sponsors of this bill, through the medium of their mortgage bonds, to be able to induce institutional lenders, who have restricted their operations to relatively large urban centres throughout Canada, to make money available to them in order to
[Mr. Howard.l	i
make mortgages freely obtainable in remote communities. This will be done in the following way.
The company will set up two funds. The first fund will be used for the purchase of N.H.A. mortgages which are government backed. Those funds will be raised by the issuing of certificates to the lenders, either trust companies or large institutional companies or individuals who lend this money to the proposed companies, for which they will in return receive certificates which can be registered as to principal or as to interest and transferrable the same as bonds. The money received in this way will be invested in N.H.A. mortgages.
The second fund will be used for conventional mortgages and, of course, certificates will be issued in the same way but the interest rates on these certificates will be slightly higher than those received in respect of the ones backed by N.H.A. loans.
That is a brief outline, but I should just like to point out that the corporation will have a capital stock of $10 million, which may be increased to $15 million, and shall be divided into shares of $10 each. At least 60 per cent of any offering of stock be reserved for a period of 15 days from the time of such offering, for the purchase by corporate or natural persons ordinarily resident in Canada. It should also be noted that not less than 75 per cent of the directors of the corporation must be Canadian citizens, ordinarily resident in Canada. The head office of the company is to be in Toronto.
I can assure hon. members that when this bill is referred to the banking and commerce committee, representatives of this proposed company will be in attendance to explain in detail its proposals, and to discuss them with anyone who is interested at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words concerning Bill No. S-16, an act to incorporate a company under the name of National Mortgage Corporation of Canada. My remarks will be brief, but I intend to pose a few questions which seem to me to require answers at this stage.
It should be noted that the petition was dated December 14, 1960 and was read on December 19, 1960. When this bill was given first reading, in the other place, on April 25, the purpose was outlined briefly. The purpose was that the company proposed to deal in mortgages of two types; those which are guaranteed by the government under C.M.H.C., and conventional mortgages. It was also stated that the company desired to raise funds for investment in N.H.A. mortgages and conventional mortgages. It is also proposed

that the company shall have the right to manage and service mortgages which are owned by its bondholders, as well as mortgages placed with the company.
Therefore, this bill provides, as the sponsor suggested this afternoon, for three main functions. One, that the proposed company be permitted to buy and sell mortgages. Two, that the company is to have the power to raise funds. Three, that the proposed company will be allowed to manage and service mortgages.
I think it will be agreed that this bill provides for a broad range of activity in the mortgage financing field in Canada. While the bill provides for activity in two separate and distinct mortgage financing fields, I cannot argue that the principle of the bill is contentious. In fact, for the past three years or more, I have urged the government to encourage the establishment of a secondary mortgage market in Canada, and on at least three occasions have set out in detail my version of an institution which could be publicly or privately owned, and would purchase N.H.A. mortgages guaranteed by the government to be used as collateral against the issuance of certificates in small denominations available to the small private investors, as well as to the large corporations. Many of these small investors, some with only a few hundred dollars, up to this point have not been able to conveniently invest in housing.
The interest rate paid on these certificates will vary with the N.H.A. fixed rate, probably one half of one per cent to three quarters of one par cent below the N.H.A. interest rate. Therefore, the series A bonds, being mortgage bonds backed by N.H.A. insured mortgages and by cash, should encourage new investors. It is my sincere hope that these mortgage bonds will be made available in small denominations, and that the greatest possible encouragement will be given the small investor to channel some of his savings in this way into the mortgage lending field. In my view it is only in this way that this corporation will be of any real benefit in bringing any new money into the mortgage lending system. Surely it cannot be argued that simply switching investment from one large corporation to another at a profit to both would contribute very much in this field. Now we have a new development and rather timely in respect of this corporation, of the government unloading C.M.H.C. mortgages at a discount which obviously will provide handsome additional profits for organizations such as the one envisaged in this bill.
A second mortgage fund to be known as mortgage fund B will be used in connection with the financing and sale of older houses,
Private Bills
we are told, and to provide funds for investment in the conventional mortgage field. It is also said that this fund will provide a suitable market for individuals, corporations and estates to sell or convert mortgages into cash. I am especially interested in the aspect of activity proposed in respect of the financing of houses already built. I would hope that we can have some clarification of what precisely is proposed in this field.
During second reading in the other place, at one point it was indicated that the fund would be used for this purpose and later that consideration would be given to ways and means of making financing available on existing houses. I would point out that there is some difference between the term "would be" and the matter of possibly giving consideration. I would hope that the hon. member who introduced this bill will be able to clear up this point. I would remind hon. members that this bill gives the corporation broad powers and once they have qualified as an approved lender under N.H.A. the company will be able to buy, sell, administer, deal in and service all mortgages coming under N.H.A. Provision is also made for investment in income-producing realty, and it will be governed by the provision of the Loan Companies Act.
As I mentioned earlier, the original petition was presented in the other place on December 19. It is of more than passing interest to note that on April 17 the Minister of Public Works made an announcement on government policy concerning the establishment of a secondary mortgage market and it is of equal interest that first reading was given to the bill in the other place on April 25, only eight days later, second reading the following day and the bill was then referred to the Senate standing committee on banking and commerce. This committee examined the bill on May 3 and third reading took place on May 10.
As a result of the careful scrutiny given this bill in the other place nine amendments of a rather technical nature were made. It is rather strange that this bill, which was so long in the drafting stage, and which had a model bill to work from, was so technically deficient when presented to the other place, unless the sponsors realized the need for haste with these new opportunities just around the corner, with the government's decision to unload $170 million worth of mortgages at a discount.
Although provisions exist in the 1954 National Housing Act for block sale of existing mortgages, there has been relatively little activity in this field up to this time. I simply pose the question that it seems a little more than coincidental that the initiative for the

Private Bills
formation of the corporation embodied in this bill has been timed so completely in accord with the government's announced policy of April 17 to unload a substantial quantity of mortgages at discounts.
My main objection to this bill arises from the proposed name, National Mortgage Corporation of Canada. The use of "National" and "of Canada" together clearly gives the impression of a government agency. I realize this matter was dealt with at some length in the other place, because I have carefully read the proceedings there. However, some very interesting evidence was presented on May 3 to the banking and commerce committee in this respect. Then later an amendment was moved on third reading in an effort by some hon. members in the other place to correct the confusion that will arise, and indeed has arisen already, as to the relationship of this corporation and the federal government. I would urge hon. members to read the objections presented to the banking and commerce committee by Mr. K. R. MacGregor, superintendent of insurance. His argument was sound and it is not my intention to delay the house by repeating or referring to his objections, nor am I going to raise the objections put forward by certain private companies such as the National Trust.
I would, however, draw hon. members' attention to the views of Dr. Stewart Bates, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and as such perhaps the person most qualified to make a recommendation in this matter. I would like to quote, if I may, from a letter of Dr. Bates.

speechtext: Well, if hon. members feel that a matter of principle is involved in the proposed name I do not want to be too technical about the discussion. I would think that one should not get into a detailed presentation of evidence on the point.

It was my intention to refer only to this one piece of evidence. It seems to me to be quite important because of the position occupied by Dr. Bates. I would quote from his letter, if I may:
Since Bill S-16 to incorporate National Mortgage Corporation of Canada was introduced in the Senate it has been brought to our attention that among approved lenders and others there is confusion as to whether this is a private corporation or a publicly owned one. In particular, we find many mortgage buyers believing this to be a government company, associated with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in connection with the recently announced government policy to develop a secondary mortgage market in Canada through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The confusion appears to stem from the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation administers the National Housing Act and insures National Housing Act loans and indeed, makes direct National Housing Act loans on its own behalf.
We believe that the confusion to which I refer is undesirable from the point of view of the sponsors of the proposed new corporation and as well, from the point of view of this corporation. We would deem it a favour if you would explore with your colleagues and the sponsors of the new corporation the necessity of having the new corporation renamed.
This is a serious request from the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and merits the serious consideration of all hon. members. As head of the corporation, Dr. Bates is possibly in the best position to assess the confusion which has arisen already and which is bound to arise in the future. Quite apart from Dr. Bate's concern about the immediate future I would also remind hon. members that governments of the future may find it necessary and desirable to set up a public corporation along these same lines. I would therefore urge that the words "National" and "of Canada" be not granted to this company to be used together in the title, one or the other would be O.K. but certainly not both together.
I do not think there is any doubt that this has caused considerable confusion. I have proof of that in the statement of the Minister of Public Works in this house on May 9 in dealing with his announcement of the first offering to the secondary mortgage market, in which he had this to say:
Prospective purchasers should therefore get in touch with one of the organizations I have just mentioned, and not with the corporation itself.
I should also like to know what the Secretary of State's department thinks about this matter. It has always been my understanding

that any words capable of giving the impression that the organization is a federal institution or a federal agency have been considered to be objectionable and have been frowned upon by the department.
I know that hon. members are aware of "Fanny May", the United States federal government company, the proper name of which is the federal national mortgage association. This, 1 suggest, is just another reason to recognize that the day may well come when we will want to form a government corporation in this particular field. What we are doing here today cannot or is not likely to be undone, and I appeal to hon. members not to grant to a private corporation a name that clearly marks it as an instrument of the federal government. Surely we are giving this corporation broad powers already and we should not be required to give it a name that would even suggest it to be an agency of our national government.
With these few general remarks, I should like to ask the sponsor a few questions. First, will this company be able to sell bonds to the banks which would yield 6 per cent and then distribute profits made on the operation of fund A, thus enabling the banks to earn more than the statutory 6 per cent allowed them under the Bank Act? Second, since the securities of this corporation, the A bonds, will be indirectly guaranteed by the government, is it not a fact that they will in effect be competing with debentures of school boards, municipalities and provinces on the one hand and at the same time getting the federal government off the hook with regard to some of its long term commitments? Normally I would not object to this form of competition but surely all hon. members are aware of the unfair treatment these junior levels of government have received as a result of the excessive borrowing of the federal government. Being absent last evening attending a function given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in tribute to the president of the general assembly of the United Nations I lost the opportunity to say a few words on the resolution preceding this bill, so I am now taking the opportunity to speak on the second reading of the bill.
We support the principles and purposes of this bill because it represents the type of farm credit legislation which members of this group have advocated for many years in this house and numerous legislatures throughout Canada. I remember being in the provincial house in company with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) just after the war began when we were advocating provincial legislation almost identical to this with respect to its interest rate and its terms of operation.
We are particularly interested in this type of legislation because we in this group are interested in the development and the welfare of the economic family farm, because we realize its place on the Canadian scene and its value to Canadian society.
The success of this legislation is clearly indicated by the fact that the minister found it necessary to introduce this bill to extend the capital available to the farm credit corporation. Its success is also indicated by its generous acceptance by the farmers and farm organizations. Because of that it is clearly indicated that it fills a long-time unfilled need in the credit sphere as far as agriculture is concerned. Personally I have been very interested for many years in long term low interest credit for farmers. In fact, I think my interest was first aroused about 1920 shortly after the first world war.
I have been on committees that studied the matter, and have been an officer of farm organizations and fruit growers' associations, during which time I have given this serious consideration. I, in association with other members, have urged the necessity for this type of legislation, at farmers' institute meetings, fruit growers' meetings, in the legislature of British Columbia, and in the House of Commons since I came here in 1945, on behalf of this group, as well as in the country since. Therefore, I have no hesitation in supporting this measure.
We believe that when the government introduces legislation which we consider advantageous to the Canadian people, we should say so and support it. When we disagree with government policy we criticize it just as harshly as we think necessary. So, after a long time, the government of Canada

Farm Credit Act
has begun to realize or accept the fact that there is a need for this type of legislation, and has done so in response to representations made by farmers' organizations in this country and by hon. members of various parties in this house over a number of years.
At the present time farm organizations and farmers generally need this type of assistance, and those who are interested in agriculture support this act and the administration. We have had a good piece of legislation in the form of this act. It is evident that it is sound because of the use that has been made of it during a very short period of time by those who have required it. Good legislation is not sufficient unless accompanied by sound administration.
Without any hesitation I wish to pay tribute to the very sound administration of this legislation by the officials of the farm credit corporation from the director to the most junior supervisor or appraiser in the field.
Why have they been able to give that good administration? I suggest first of all it is because the great majority have that "something" which is required to make this type of legislation a success. They have a feeling for agriculture, and the experience in this field which gives them the knowledge of the farmers' problems, which is required. I suggest therein lies the basis for sound judgment when it comes to the question of assisting to meet farmers' needs in respect to credit.
In addition to that, not only have they this feeling for agriculture, and experience, but the staff has had much imagination and many ideas, while at the same time they have kept their feet on the ground. This is very different from the administration of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I am not blaming the board or personnel, but that act was administered under the Department of Finance. It is very peculiar that whenever this type of act is administered under the Department of Finance it is not as successful as it might otherwise be, because it is being administered by people who think in terms of money and interest rather than personal relationships, land development and so on. However, that situation is inevitable. The act was too restrictive in its application and it did not provide to those administering it the opportunity to exercise their imaginations, nor to put into operation their ideas, as this act does. There was too little contact with applicants after loans had been made and very little in the way of an advisory staff in partnership with the farmers in their day to day operations after they had become clients of the board. That situation has changed entirely.

As far as the local administration is concerned, I have noticed a big difference in the administration of this act compared with that of the Canadian farm loan board, and I have had quite a long time experience with the Canadian farm loan board. I am by no means flattered by that suggestion, Mr. Speaker. I represent the dairy farmers, the beef farmers, the small general farmers, the fruit farmers, the poultry farmers, the muskrat farmers, and so on. I want to make a few suggestions in this connection but they are not particularly critical. I realize the difficulties at the present time with respect to the administrative load that is being placed on the headquarters staff.
I do suggest to the minister that within reason every opportunity be presented to the senior staff of headquarters, the director and his close associates, to make more frequent visits to different parts of Canada, to visit the local offices and become as acquainted as they can personally with the various regions of the various provinces and the areas within the provinces under their jurisdiction. I think it would be very worth while from their point of view and from the point of view of the farmers they are aiming to serve. I think this brings the administration close to the people and everything should be done toward that end. I particularly suggest that they do not overlook the Kootenays, because there they can do business and enjoy themselves at the same time. You can actually fish, troll or fly-fish in a boat as you go along from one farm to another around these beautiful lakes. It is a combination of business and recreation.
Then I suggest that senior officials and the provincial and district officials, where the opportunity occurs under suitable circumstances, attend farmers' meetings and the meetings of other organizations. As far as the farm organization meetings are concerned, I am thinking particularly of the local farm level, the local farmers' institute, the local federations of agriculture, the local fruit growers' association, and so forth. I urge them to attend those meetings and inform them fully of the purposes of the legislation and maintain that close contact and co-operation.
This type of legislation to serve the country to the best advantage also requires cooperation from the top right down to the individual farmers and through them the farmers' organizations because even skilled administrators and ministers can learn from people in very humble circumstances who have the capacity to observe, form judgments and pass on their information to others.

Farm Credit Act
I may say, Mr. Speaker, one of the main reasons why I utter so many, or give vent to so many, wise suggestions in this house and express so many good ideas is that I am fed continually by the people I represent in Kootenay West. They furnish me with these ideas and I simply rise in my place and act as their spokesman.
Then again I suggest also that the senior officials and the district officials, particularly the senior officials, should take the opportunity to visit on a spot basis certain typical farms in each of the areas they visit so that they will get a pretty close understanding of local circumstances.
I have one further suggestion. I can see possibilities in this direction. I presume there has not been a great deal of experience with this up to date. I understand it is quite possible for forest farmers to secure a loan under proper circumstances, as any other farmer can do, from the farm credit corporation. This is a thing I am very interested in and a good number of my constituents are interested in forest farms. I think you call them woodlots in Ontario. It is an area in our country of anything from say 100 acres up to 2,000, 3,000 or 5,000 acres of timber which a man is farming and cropping. Under the legislation I understand it is possible for a person with satisfactory security and knowledge of his business to obtain a loan if he satisfies the requirements of the act. I do suggest it would be a good idea if some of the senior officials would give some thought to this type of application. It takes a person with a little bit of experience, a man who is able to cruise timber and measure it. If a farmer says, "I have 5 million feet of timber on this property," he must be able to confirm that there are 5 million feet. It takes a man who understands species, who understands accessibility of timber, the markets, the cost of building roads and the possibilities for the development of, say, a local lumber market or other forest products market, or shipping to outside markets. In view of the possible future developments in that direction, I do suggest that it is a very worth while feature of farm technology and that more consideration be given to making certain that there are some of the officials of the farm credit corporation who have a knowledge of forest farming in all its aspects.
This is all I have to say at this time. I may have a word or two to say later on but I see nothing to criticize in the legislation, nothing to criticize so far as the administration is concerned to date and I think the best way to show my appreciation to the minister at this time is to conclude at this point.
