I should like for a few minutes to add my words of support for this measure. As one who represents a district where farming is perhaps a little different from that in most areas may I say I am sure hon. members will appreciate the difficulties that are found in an area where a family farm can consist of one acre covered with glass or maybe 1,500 acres used as a ranch. It could be land used for tobacco at $1,000 an acre in value or land that could be used for pasture purposes, heavy land, worth approximately $60 an acre.
Hon. members will appreciate that in administering a measure such as the farm credit corporation legislation the administrators are faced with immense problems. Under the previous administration there was not a great deal of desire on the part of the farmers, because of the high price of land, to use the implements at hand because it was felt that the money involved did not represent a large enough sum to help them obtain the necessary loan that would make such a venture profitable. When the act was amended to make it possible for young men to borrow up to $20,000 at 5 per cent from the farm credit corporation and to obtain additional funds for machinery and livestock under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it was quite apparent that the young farmers in the riding of Kent felt that they at last had the tools necessary to help them obtain a farm loan.
One of the basic problems that faced these young, progressive, scientific farmers when they began to take advantage of these loans was the time lag. A great deal of time elapsed from the time they applied for a loan until it was processed and the money was actually placed at their disposal. There was considerable concern over this time lag and a desire to know where to place the blame. I too was very interested because of the many representations made to me and so I took the opportunity of going through the district to try to ascertain where the blame lay. Much to my amazement and to the amazement of other people concerned I found that the main reason for the delay was the tremendous number of applications being placed in the office by farmers wishing to take advantage of this legislation. It was absolutely impossible for the staff then available to process so many applications more rapidly. Let me assure you that these people were highly experienced and competent because of their association with the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. They simply had too many loans to process in too short a time.
However, when the thing began to roll the time lag became shorter and shorter, and I am very happy to report now that there are

very few instances indeed where the young man is held up to any extent on this account. One of the most amazing things that occurred when some of these young men made applications for loans was that they did not always get the amount for which they applied. Any man who has dealings with a bank will very often find that he does not get what he asks for; but in connection with these applications these people in some instances did not obtain what they asked for but rather much more than the amount for which they applied.
I should like to refer to one young farmer with whom I am acquainted. He made application for a loan of $9,000. The men who administer the act are very competent farm managers themselves. They were able to point out to this young farmer that he could put his farm in a much more stable position, thus making it possible for him to repay the loan much sooner, give his farm a better rating and provide his family with a better living if he would borrow more money than the amount for which he had applied. This farmer who had applied for a loan of $9,000 was actually granted a loan of $20,000 by the farm credit corporation, and today he is one of the most progressive young men in the area.
I should like to lend my support to this measure for one basic reason. For too long we have seen the best and most energetic young men leaving the farms and going to the cities to take positions in industry simply because they lacked the necessary funds to purchase their fathers' farms. These fathers had worked through the years to pay off their farms and in many instances there were still small mortgages left. These young men were unable to take over their fathers' farms and so they went into industry and the farms passed into the hands of strangers.
I am very happy to report that in my district the situation seems to have reversed. The young men feel that at last here is an opportunity to borrow a large amount of money at a reasonable rate of interest over a suitable period of time. Thus they are given a reasonable opportunity to pay back the loan with honour, and thanks to the farm credit corporation legislation they feel they can obtain the necessary amount to buy the family farm which means so much to them, land which they are accustomed to work and on which they can do the best job.
I think we have in my riding one of the finest examples in Canada today of young men at last being able to remain on the family farm because they feel that it will carry them and their families into the future with the same degree of security and satisfaction that was experienced by their parents.

At last there is a source of credit that is of value to the young men in my area and enables them to attain a business of their own. They have the desire and the knowledge and now they have the funds. This measure makes it possible for them to achieve success in life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night and again tonight the minister gave us a detailed summary of the operation of the Farm Credit Act which is the old farm loans act under a new name, and his summary was very useful indeed. However, I wish to submit a few suggestions which, if taken into consideration and acted upon, will help not only the farmers of my constituency but farmers on small holdings everywhere.
The actual effect of this legislation is to increase the amount available for lending from $200 million to $300 million. I am heartily in favour of the principle of the bill and therefore I am not going to criticize the principle but rather some aspects of the administration of the legislation. As I realize that the bill under discussion would mean the enactment of legislation which could be of assistance to the agricultural potential of the district of Thunder Bay in which my constituency is located, I desire to avail myself of the opportunity to participate briefly m the discussion in the hope that I may be able to impress upon the minister the importance of doing something more than is being done at present by the senior levels of government to bring the agricultural lands of the district, ^ which, as everyone knows, are not a prairie type of soil, into productive holdings from which our farmers can make a decent living.
I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the district is not known as a prosperous agricultural area. It has within its confines a few very fine, well developed and productive farms. The great majority, however, are comparatively small holdings of anywhere from 100 to 300 acres.
One of the commendable aspects of this bill is to provide assistance to those on the land who would otherwise be unable to obtain loans in the ordinary way. This is a welcome measure, especially for those who will be able to qualify; but the farmers of my district have had very little success in obtaining loans to improve their farms in the past.
I have already indicated that the average farmer in my constituency cultivates a comparatively small parcel of land. The majority are of the dairy and truck garden variety. We have, however, large tracts of empty barren areas that could profitably be put

Farm Credit Act
to farm use if the prospective farmer had the means of acquiring stock and machinery.
From its inception the farm loan act the name of which was changed to the Farm Credit Act has provided the means for financing farm equipment to western farmers. But it has not been too prone to do so for the poor farmers of the east, notably those in my constituency, with the result that they have had to resort to finance companies for their purchases of machinery, paying a rate of interest considerably higher than they would have had to pay had they been able to borrow from the banks through the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
During the past decade we have witnessed a trend of movement from the rural to the urban centres, brought about by more attractive living conditions, which in no small measure, have been due to gainful employment which up to two or three years ago it was rather easy to obtain. Conditions are now somewhat reversed in many cases and therefore I believe that what we should be concerned with at present is stimulating an interest in a return to the land movement. That is something which, in my opinion, we must do sooner or later.
Speaking on the supply motion on agriculture in 1960, as reported at page 3427 of Hansard I made the following statement:
I have said previously and I say again that unless a farmer in our district has sufficient collateral to show it is next to impossible for him to secure a loan to enable him to develop efficiently and economically the agricultural potential of his holding.
The situation as described is just as true today as it was a year ago. I have been pleading with the government for easier credits for our farmers ever since my election to parliament in 1958, and I shall continue to do so until the tillers of the soil of my constituency receive the same consideration as do their more fortunate counterparts in the prairie provinces and in the lush eastern parts of Ontario. Social workers, clergymen and others agree that the farm and village are the ideal setting for family life, the best of all places in which to bring up a family. But, so long as a lack of opportunity for financial improvement exists, and so long as inability to borrow money from lending institutions continues, individual poverty and lack of community resources will drive farming people to the urban areas where, instead of milk and honey, only crowded conditions and often misery prevail.
Our efforts should be directed toward building a happy rural Canada instead of discouraging people from living on the farm, thus leading them to the misery of unemployment in the cities.

As a result of neglect on the part of both senior levels of government, both federal and provincial, during the past 20 years, the number of farmers in the Thunder Bay district decreased from approximately 2,500 to about half that number or 1,250, and a considerable portion of the land which they farmed is now deserted and looks as though a hurricane had passed through it leaving behind nothing but buildings which look like derelicts.
I think that the role in the economy of the farmer who operates a mixed holding of a few hundred acres or less has been overlooked by the government. Not sufficient emphasis has been forthcoming from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) in the way of promotion, especially in undeveloped areas such as the lakehead district which has a population of 125,000, of which only 5.3 per cent are farmers, whereas for the province of Ontario the percentage of farmers to the total population is about 12J per cent.
The advent of the seaway, now in its third year of operation, has increased the demand for fresh farm produce. Unlimited supply of livestock feed is available at lakehead terminals. The disadvantage appears to be small amounts of crop land. There are plenty of good prospective farmers as well as those who are now on the land who would wish to enlarge and improve their holdings in order to get the maximum return from their land, and the only thing that stops them is lack of capital. If this increase in the capital of the farm credit corporation is really going to be made available to needy farmers and prospective farmers, then I would certainly congratulate the minister on his too little but, I hope, not too late measure to rescue the type of farmer for whom I am speaking.
I am a staunch advocate of a liberal credit policy designed to encourage ownership and operation of farms, large and small, in every part of Canada. Among the small farmers of northwestern Ontario is the mixed farmer who keeps cows, grows vegetables and has a woodlot from which he derives the biggest part of his income by selling the pulpwood to the local pulp and paper companies. These farmers should be assisted in setting up projects of reforestation. I express the hope that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) will take under advisement the establishment of a policy to encourage reforestation on lands owned by these small woodlot farmers. This is the type of farmer that predominates in the agricultural areas of northwestern Ontario.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am trying to bring to the attention of the house ways in which I believe this legislation could help our farmers. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that in order to establish a 5 cans of milk quota an investment of from $30,000 to $40,000 is required. This would gross to the farmer the princely sum of only $20 per day. As everyone knows, the farmer must of necessity milk his cows 12 hours apart, seven days a week, 52 weeks a year, notwithstanding the mechanization which has taken place in recent years.
One of the greatest problems of the farmer today is finding the money for the operation of his farm in the face of heavy payments on his capital expenditure for the mechanization
Farm Credit Act
of his operation, which mechanization has been forced upon him due to the difficulty of securing part-time farm help.
Farm loans have taken the place of the hired man. The farmer now hires money instead of men to carry on his farm operations. Of course, if he cannot borrow money his enterprise will suffer. It is for this reason the government has realized that more money is needed, and I am all for it.
I would feel much happier, of course, if those responsible for the approval of these loans took into consideration all factors, not least of which is the essential need of the individual applicant, regardless of geography. In the northern Ontario area there are a number of French speaking farmers, which would justify the appointment of a bilingual inspector of farm holdings whose job it is to approve loan applications. The point is that applications are often turned down because of a lack of understanding of the farmer's problems and because there is not a proper appreciation of the relative value of farms in these rugged parts of Ontario.
Local banks, while sympathetic, will loan money under the farm loan act. However, they will only loan amounts which are not necessarily based on needs, but rather on the bank's evaluation of the farmer as a financial risk. It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture should initiate a study of all the potentials of agriculture in every part of Canada, instead of confining most of his attention to the problems of the big western farmers. The farm credit corporation should be able to recommend applications for loans to any farmer or farm organization for the establishment of facilities which would help not only farmers but the economy of the area in which these facilities will be located.
Loans are required to assist farmers to acquire registered livestock. If they had the money, they would be in a position to buy a better class of cattle. This is just as important in agriculture as it is for a factory to have better machinery with which to improve its products. According to the annual report in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act for the year 1960, in the 15 years since the act was introduced, from 1945 to 1960, out of a total of $1,013,782,000 borrowed under the act there remains outstanding $177 million, represented by 170 loans. Practically all the money borrowed from 1945 to 1956 has been repaid. This is the point I wish to bring out. On the basis of this record no one can deny the wisdom of the government of the day in enacting this legislation, the results of which have been an outstanding success.
The submission of the national farmers' union made to the government on February

Farm Credit Act
15, 1961, rejected the widely held opinion that technology and efficiency demand the removal of the majority of farm families from the land. The brief included these words:
We do not subscribe to the theory that the activities and institutions ol men are determined solely by technology and economics regardless of human and social values, but hold that technological developments can and must be adjusted to serve the human, social and economic needs of men.
We believe that the family farm is the most efficient unit in terms not only of production, but also in terms of soil conservation and human and social values. We therefore believe that the preservation of the family farm is of importance to farm families as well as to the nation as a whole.
I for one certainly subscribe to these sentiments, which are opposed to the farm people of Canada becoming "factory in the field" instead of a happy family farm. Canada's best interests will be served in the end by a large number of mixed farms rather than by a few specialized farm units.
It seems to me that the flight from the farm to the city which has been going on over the past several years is a sad trend. This decline in our farm population and in the relative importance of agriculture to the national economy is to be regretted. Certainly it has its sad side, particularly for those whose roots are deep in the land.
Our farm population may continue to shrink. The farmer is unlikely to become extinct, however, because he has an important role to play in the Canadian economy for a long time to come; just as long, in fact, as human beings need to eat.
With modern aids life on the farm is undoubtedly easier than it has ever been. The advent of the automobile, telephone, radio, television, the differences between rural and urban living have been narrowed to the point that a "back to the land" campaign would not be a bad idea. I commend this to the minister. If this bill will do anything to encourage people to stay on the farm and encourage some to settle on the land, then I say it will have accomplished a great deal for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if the sentiments expressed by the last speaker truly represent the views of the official opposition, I am very happy to learn that the Liberal party has at long last discovered the value and virtues of the family farmer.
In considering whether or not support should be given to legislation of this kind which, in effect, will have the result of increasing by $100 million the amount of money available for lending under this legislation, I think one is driven to consider what were the simple principles which encouraged the government to pass the legislation in the

first place. In order to recapitulate these I can do no better than read briefly from a statement made by Mr. George Owen, chief of the loans division of the corporation to the banker's summer school in Guelph. I am paraphrasing and summarizing the statement but I think it is constructive and I should like to put a few paragraphs on the record. These are simple principles but there is a tendency for us to stray away from them. When legislation has been passed we are inclined to look only at the means of applying the legislation and sometimes we forget the principles which led to its introduction. I am quoting now:
The farmer, looking for ways and means of increasing his net income, has little hope of increasing prices for his product. There seems to be even less possibility that the cost of the items he must buy, in order to produce, will be less. His only real hope appears to lie in producing a greater volume of high-quality, readily-marketable product, thus spreading overhead costs over a larger number of units, and in careful planning and organization to reduce operating costs.
Higher wages in industry have made it almost impossible to hire farm labour at a price the farmer can afford, and a shortage of labour in the production season adds to the risk of depending on hired labour. Farm labour which could be paid for by the day, week or month has, therefore, been largely replaced by machinery, which must be paid for in cash or with credit.
Fortunately, with modern machinery and laboursaving methods, farmers may now handle much larger units. The cost of setting up a minimum economic family farm unit has thus greatly increased over the years. What is equally important is the fact that the capital structure of the individual farm has changed, with a higher percentage of total assets being represented by livestock, equipment and working capital, and a lesser percentage by real property, which has been the traditional security for long term credit. As a result, the credit arrangements which could be made under the former Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, either separately or together, although fairly adequate for the well-established farmer, became entirely inadequate to meet the needs of the capable farmer on a farm of limited size who wishes to expand his unit, or of a young and capable farmer desirous of setting up an economic farm unit.
I think it was for the purpose which those last few sentences have defined that this legislation was passed. It has proved a most valuable asset to the farmers, as I know from my personal knowledge, and for this reason I have no hesitation at all in adding my support to this particular bill.
Dealing with the measure from a narrower angle, let me say that I have made it my business as I go home to talk to the people who have made applications, who have been granted loans or whose applications are being processed. I would estimate that I have seen or visited or written letters to approximately 25 per cent of those farmers in my constituency who have been in contact with the officials of the farm credit corporation with respect to this legislation and there is not

the slightest doubt that the benefits which have been brought to these farmers are invaluable. As I say, I am speaking from my own experience. I am not going to deal with this subject statistically because I do not think dealing with it on a statistical basis would lend colour to our reasons for supporting this legislation. These are living people we are dealing with, working farmers, many of whom I have met.
In my area particularly under the old administration-I do not place any particular blame upon them, but it did happen-some of the officials of the farm loans board responsible for policy completely refused to acknowledge that farmers could be successful if they carried on their operations some miles from rail head. In what is called the Battle river district, some 60 miles north of the Grimshaw area through which the new railway will go, a splendid farming community has been built up, but only within the last two or three years has it been possible for the people of that district to have the benefit of this farm credit legislation made available to them. These benefits will, I hope, in due course be extended even further up into the Fort Vermilion area between 200 and 250 miles from the railroad.
Another aspect of this legislation I should like to praise is the time spent by the officials in preliminary assessment and appraisal. In the old days people would make applications for loans and send in their forms. Then there would usually be an attempt to cut down the amount of the loan to some extent without too much regard for the purpose for which the loan has been made. I think that was entirely wrong. It is a fault which has certainly been cured by the present legislation and the machinery for administering it. I know from my experience that the officials spend a great deal of time counselling and assisting the farmers and making recommendations concerning the type of loan they should have, the amount they should ask for and the purpose for which it should be granted, not in an arbitrary or authoritarian way but as helpers and advisers. I think this has paid off and that it will continue to pay off in the future.
My colleague who spoke before me mentioned the flexibility of the machinery of legislation and the willingness of the officials, should the circumstances justify it, to increase the amount of a loan which had been made in order to meet the exigencies of a particular situation; their willingness to take into account the human factor. I can recall last summer receiving a telephone call and, later, a visit from a middle aged farmer who had made an application for a loan which had been rejected. He did not come to me in
Farm Credit Act
order to complain, but he wanted to know whether anything further could be done. This was obviously a borderline case and in certain conditions he might well have been eligible. From what I knew of him I was satisfied that he was a suitable person to receive a loan. I telephoned the head office and within 24 hours another official came out, there was a reappraisal of the land in the light of certain conditions which I knew, and, as a result, in less than three days this application had been accepted. This is an illustration that knowledge of the human beings concerned in these transactions can, in itself, be enough to justify placing an application in a category where it can be accepted.
Another thing which appeals to me in connection with this legislation and its administration is the provision made for decentralization. I mentioned this before in connection with the A.R.D.A. bill which the Minister of Agriculture brought in. Undoubtedly it is necessary for governments to take unto themselves a large degree of power and authority. They have to do so in the complex world in which we live. But it is my conviction that wherever possible the use of such power should be decentralized and the right to make decisions should be left as far as possible with the officials in the field who are calculated to have a more precise knowledge of what the real facts are. All too often, by the time applications had been processed by a system of intellectual osmosis from the perimeter to Ottawa and back again weeks had elapsed, the tenor of the application had been destroyed and its urgency entirely dissipated. I know for a fact that a large amount of control and authority is left with the officials who are in the field. So far in my experience, they have made good and adequate use of it. That is another reason which I advance for supporting the legislation.
I could mention a number of cases, perhaps 25 per cent or 30 per cent in my constituency, where this program has been effective, but I shall not take up the time of this house to do so.
I know that while there are no figures or information available as to the exact aomunt of loans which have been made, they are quite substantial. I am satisfied for the reasons I have advanced that many of the people who were entitled to loans found that their rights to a loan have been restricted by the regulations of the old farm loan board, which considered the applications from this area, and I should think that because of this, under the new act we have probably had as large a number of applications from that area as from any other constituency in Canada, and I think that will continue for some time.

Farm Credit Act
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but put on the record my feeling that the family farm, with the individual farmer, is probably one of the important remaining strongholds of the principles of human freedom, enterprise and liberty. I am not suggesting that it is the only stronghold, but the man and family who have to contend with nature with their own resources, represent an institution which, in our struggle with the other half of the world, we must strengthen and perpetuate.
I read just the other day in a news item that a large quantity of land in Russia has been turned over to collective farming, where because of the fact that there had not been that care and regard which the individual farmer has for his own land, machinery and stock, that land, which probably should never have been put under the plough, had seriously deteriorated. As a result, the estimates of the U.S.S.R., in anticipation of their food requirements, were much higher than could be produced, and they were sadly disappointed. I suggest that illustrates the absolute necessity for strengthening and maintaining, as an underpinning of our economy and way of life, the family farm of our country, because from there will be fed those qualities of industry, initiative and enterprise which have injected into the bloodstream of the nation those things which will perpetually keep us strong and maintain us in our present economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. E. Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having been in this house for many years I can assure hon. members that because this farm loan corporation comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) and because I am his parliamentary secretary, I feel it my duty to say a few words to strengthen his hand.
This is the best farm loan corporation that has ever existed in the Dominion of Canada during my lifetime. It has been brought forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), the leader of this government, to assist farmers to assist themselves. We are now in a position where any farmer who has the qualifications can secure this type of loan without any difficulty.
I have been farming all my life and have paid for a farm the hard way, by borrowing the money from the bank at too high a rate of interest. I suggest 5 per cent interest is the highest rate that farmers can afford to pay, if thew are to be able to pay back the loan. The farmers must certainly pay back the loans because when they borrow from the farm loan corporation it is made abundantly clear to them that unless they prove 
that they are able to pay back the loan with interest within a certain number of years the loans will be refused.
We have the advantage now that many farmers who previously were unable to obtain a loan find they can do so through the farm loan corporation at 5 per cent interest, and thereby are able to increase their ability to pay back the loan.
I come from a part of the country which is purely agricultural. The farmers of that area have borrowed over $1 million from this corporation since its inception. Many townships have borrowed much more than others, but in my county farmers have been able to borrow well over a million dollars. In the province of Ontario loans to the extent of $23,011,870 have been made.
I should like to draw to the attention of this house some figures which I obtained from the latest full report of the farm credit corporation, for the years 1959-60. I intend to give the figures for a period of five years, from 1955 to 1960.
The number of loans approved in 1955-56 was 2,057; in 1956-57, 2,921; 1957-58, 3,702; 1958-59, 4,805 and in 1959-60, 5,339. The difference in the number of loans during that five year period is 3,282.

speechtext:
The farmers have been able to obtain that many more loans in 1960 than they were able to obtain in 1955. That is exactly what it means.
The average amount of the loans in 1955 was $4,040 while the average of the loans in 1960 is $7,498, which is almost double. The difference is $3,458. The total amount of approved loans in 1955 was $8,309,650, while the total amount in 1960 was $40,031,250, the difference being $31,721,600.
The farmers are not receiving anything for nothing because they must pay 5 per cent interest. This is not a hand-out in any way to the farmer.
I should like to explain how farm loans can be used. First, they can be used to acquire farmland and to erect or modernize farm buildings. Second, they can be used to purchase basic herd livestock and necessary farm equipment. Third, they can be used to provide lime, fertilizer and seed to establish permanent plantings. Fourth, they can be used to discharge liabilities, or for any purpose which the corporation considers necessary for the organization and operation of an economic family farm unit.
I should like now to give a few more figures by placing the following quotation on the record:

On March 31, I960, there were outstanding 28,453 first mortgage loans totalling $119,978,763, and 505 second mortgage loans totalling $173,108. In addition, the corporation held 91 sale agreements valued at $83,256 and 12 parcels of real estate in which the corporation's investment is $31,346 carried at a book value of $21,373. The following table shows the number of mortgage loans outstanding and the corporation's investment in them in each of the last five years, including accrued interest to March 31 each year.

Year	Loans	Investment1955/56	18,931	$ 44,958,1361956/57	20,372	53,748,3641957/58	22,494	68,490,5231958/59	25,471	91,298,1191959/60	28,453	120,151,871
At the end of the fiscal year 90.9 per cent of all first mortgage loan accounts were in good standing, as compared with 91.4 per cent on March 31, 1959. A total of $7,903,633 of principal was repaid during the year, of which 67.4 per cent was received in payment of principal not yet due. Interest due during the year amounted to $4,443,338, of which $4,111,165, or 92.5 per cent had been paid by the end of the year.
Types of Mortgage Loan The Farm Credit Act provides two types of long term mortgage loans to bona fide and competent farmers, who are in actual need of assistance to set up economic farm units, the income from which is largely derived from crops grown on such units, and marketed either directly or through livestock. The first, under part II of the act, is an extension of the assistance formerly available from the Canadian farm loan board. It is based on the security of farm land and may be made to persons whose principal occupation is farming. The maximum loans may not exceed 75 per cent (formerly 65 per cent) of the value of the farm land taken as security or $20,000 (formerly $15,000), whichever is the lesser. These loans are repayable by equal annual or semi-annual instalments of combined principal and interest over an appropriate period not to exceed 30 years.
The second, under part III of the act, is designed to assist young farmers who have attained the age of 21 years and have not attained the age of 45 years, and who have at least five years' farming experience, to become established on economic farm units. Such loans are based primarily on first mortgage security of farm lands, but up to 40 per cent of the required security may be represented by livestock and farm equipment. The maximum loan may not exceed 75 per cent of the value of the farm land and chattels taken as security or $27,500, whichever is the lesser. That portion of the loan secured by farm land is repayable over a period not to exceed 30 years, and that portion (if any) which is based on chattel security must be repaid within the first 10 years. Part III loans are further secured by insurance on the life of the borrower. Another new and significant feature of these loans is the provision of supervision by the corporation of the borrower's farming operations until such time as the loan has been reduced to 65 per cent of the appraised value of the farm land held as security.
I should like to put on the record the cost of making and administering loans:
As of March 31, 1960, the average interest being paid on all money on loan to the corporation was 4.2 per cent. However, since the reserve, amounting to $3,748,862, and the capital of the corporation, 90205-6-398
Farm Credit Act
amounting to $5 million, are available for loaning without interest cost to the corporation, the average interest cost of all money on loan to borrowers at that date was 3.9 per cent.
If, as expected, the corporation is obliged to borrow $50 million in the fiscal year 1960-61, and assuming that the interest rate on new money is that now prevailing, the average interest rate on the total money available for loaning purposes will be approximately 4.45 per cent as of March 31, 1961. This would leave a margin between the average cost of money to the corporation and the interest charged to its borrowers of only 0.55 per cent as compared with an average annual operating cost over the past five years of 1.1 per cent.
The corporation will derive additional revenue from the increased appraisal fees payable on new applications, but this will be more than offset by the cost of the extra staff required to make and review appraisals, which is made necessary by the much greater risks inherent in the provisions of the new legislation, and to supply a pre-loan counselling and loan service to farmers in their own communities. Additional costs will also be involved in bringing salaries in line with those being paid for similar work within the civil service.
I do not wish to read any more. I have had a lot of experience with farm loans and with the Veterans' Land Act from 1940 to 1945 when soldiers overseas came back to be re-established. I have had a lot of experience with the farm loan board and now this act has come into being. I can assure the house that if loans under this act increase in the next three years, as they have in the past years, they will more than double in a very short time. I would say that in a year the number of loans will be double what they are now. This proves that the farmers themselves have accepted this act and are taking advantage of it.

Mr. Speaker, the Farm Credit Act is very popular in British Columbia. Some 355 applications have been received and according to the latest figures there are 25 now pending. To date about 16 per cent of the applications have been rejected. The total amount of loans in British Columbia is $3,469,150 for some 254 loans, or an average of about $13,700 per loan. I believe that Fraser Valley tops the list in the province for the number of loans made with the Okanagan Boundary district coming second.
As Fraser Valley is the centre of a large dairy industry, it is an area where farm loans are often required. The large co-operative Fraser Valley milk producers' association does big business in this area amounting to some $27 million a year. High-class cattle are bred here and although sales there do not average as high as the figure of $1,790, which was reached in Ontario recently at the national sale, the cattle that are bred do furnish considerable revenue along with the revenue from milk production.
I had one rejection of a loan brought to my attention before I came here last fall. A young man had received a farm of 225 acres with excellent soil because of the death of his mother and he wanted to borrow $20,000 on the farm. There were no mortgages on the farm at the time and I was rather amazed when he telephoned me one day and said that

his loan application had been refused. I discussed the matter with the supervisor and he informed me that he considered that this man was trying to run an uneconomic operation. There were two hired men on the farm in addition to the owner and they were milking 30 cows. It is a poor man these days who cannot milk 30 cows himself, let alone having three men doing the job. This application was turned down but the young man then borrowed the money privately elsewhere.
In discussing the Farm Credit Act I think we should consider both the pros and cons, and if I am a little critical I hope the minister will forgive me. It may be because of the hot, sultry weather we are having but I do feel somewhat critical tonight about certain features of the act. I believe the chief criticism of the act in British Columbia is the difficulty of getting a loan on a small acreage, say 10 acres. Holdings of that size may be operated as poultry, berry, vegetable, flower, seed or even holly farms. A poultryman does not require heavy, fertile soil. In fact, for drainage purposes often poorer soil is better than rich soil. On the other hand, a berry crop requires a good soil. These are opposite situations but it shows the difference that can be found in 10-acre farms. It is amazing how much a revenue can be derived from 10 acres under certain circumstances.
I believe that at the commencement of the operation of the act the idea was that a poultryman should produce on the property half the feed that he uses. Hence he needed more than just a small acreage and this was one of the reasons why applications were turned down. This is an erroneous idea. Grain may be purchased in Fraser valley and in fact in most of British Columbia much more cheaply than it can be grown, especially on small farms and crop failures could be common especially in wet weather. This is a very poor idea but if my information is correct, at the present time I believe this clause has now been more or less eliminated and it is up to the supervisor as to whether he thinks there is a prospect of this particular farmer, whether he is a poultryman, a dairyman, or a fruit grower, can make a success of the venture.
The small dairy farmer is a different proposition. So, as I say, anything that has a reasonable chance of success is likely to be passed by the supervisor. A loan on a farm that is not operating successfully should be turned down anyway. Where farmers cannot succeed, it is often necessary to move or at least for the sons to seek employment elsewhere.
This is where vocational training schools fit into the picture of the farm loan board.
90205-6-398J
Farm Credit Act
The vocational training school project has gradually caught fire. I note that Ontario is planning an $8 million building program to be completed during the next year and a half. This will accommodate many students from farms as well as other places and even the actual labour of building will, it is stated, provide employment for about 20,000 workers for 18 months. In a local paper from British Columbia recently I noted a report stating that the minister of education has planned to spend $10 million on enlarging vocational schools in agricultural areas in order to look after certain instruction to young farmers and farmers' daughters. Some farms in British Columbia are well adapted for recreation centres around a lake or for motels or camp sites, et cetera. A dude ranch might be more profitable than is more standard farming. This whole system is suitable for arranging just such things as these. All these features should be investigated by the owner in order to see whether increased revenue, some of it easy money, could not be picked up. If failure is sure on any farm, no loan should be given.
Another criticism in Fraser valley and the coast area occurred when the provincial head office was moved from New Westminster to Kelowna. It was moved without notice and to the minds of many, for very little reason. It was asserted that it was nearer the centre of British Columbia. This is incorrect because Vanderhoof is the centre of the province. It was asserted that there were more loans in this area. I believe this statement was incorrect. It was asserted that it was nearer the farming area. May I say that Fraser Valley produces a great deal of farm revenue. I am sure there is agreement on that matter. Mr. Speaker, last night when we listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) speak and again tonight I think we realized that he gave a rather concise picture of the operation of the farm credit corporation and of the need to increase the authorized capital of the corporation itself. Those of us who represent farm constituencies realize at first hand the need for this increase in capital because of the great demand for the service which the corporation is rendering. In an area such as that which I represent, where the assessment ranges from $500 a quarter section to $5,000, you can well realize the difficulty in the operation, and the assessment and the appraisal of the applications which come in. However, I have been greatly impressed by the enthusiasm not only of the staff and the officials of the farm credit corporation but by the responsibility which the applicants feel towards the officials of the farm credit corporation. It makes a person realize that the staff and the officials who are administering the act and working for the corporation really believe in them wholeheartedly. They impress upon the applicants the possibilities which are theirs within the scope of the act and the great way in which the farmers can avail themselves of the various opportunities.
When we look at the figures very briefly for the last three years, Mr. Speaker, we can realize why this authorization is required. In 1958, when the farm loan board was in effect, the loans made that year amounted to $30 million. In the following year, when the farm loan board was operated and the farm credit corporation took over after October 5, the loans rose to $40 million. In this last year for which we have records the loans are up to $60 million.
There has been very little increase in the staff during those three years. It is fairly obvious that the services which are rendered by the staff of the farm credit corporation are really outstanding. I refer primarily to the pre-loan counselling which is given by the farm credit corporation advisers. These officials are devoted servants. They are intelligent and they certainly have dedication to the work which they are doing. As I say, they impress the farmers very greatly and they are able to interpret the provisions of the

act in a most admirable manner. The farmers who benefit by the clauses of the act realize that here is something which can improve their position. They are now able to get adequate credit which for many years had been denied them. They are aware that under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture we have a corporation which is serving a crying need that had been denied for a long time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see the evening is wearing on and in rising at this time it is not my purpose to delay the second reading of this bill. However, I do have some brief comments to make on farm credit legislation.
I think that before looking at Canada's new farm credit legislation we might look at the farm credit situation as it existed prior to the introduction of these measures, and at some of the reasons why legislative changes appeared necessary if agriculture was to be given a chance to take advantage of the new technologies and methods which have been found so effective in reducing agricultural costs.
The amount of capital required to set up a minimum economic family farm unit having more than doubled since the last war, the credit arrangements which could be made under the Canadian farm loan act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, either separately or together, although fairly adequate for the well established farmer were entirely inadequate to meet the needs of the young and capable farmer desirous of setting up an economic family farm unit unless, of course, he was fortunate enough to possess at least 50 per cent of the required capital or a minimum of $15,000.
To start out with something less than an economic family farm unit meant higher production costs in the beginning, and consequently very little by way of profit with which to expand. The struggle toward such a unit had become so slow that only a fortunate few ever reached it in time to fully exploit its advantages and, because of its cost, it was a difficult unit to dispose of in its entirety or even to transfer from one generation to another without the intervention of very substantial credit. The result has been that the transition to the family farm unit of economic size capable of using modern methods and of producing a standard, readily marketable product at a minimum cost has, in most parts of this country, been extremely slow.
There seemed to be good reason to believe that the problems associated with low farm income and with surplus disposal were closely linked with relatively high production costs,

and that these excess costs were largely due to the fact that by far the greater number of Canadian farms were still a long way from being economic units by present day standards. It also seemed evident that lack of capital was making it difficult for farmers in the more adaptable areas to switch production from straight grain farming and in so doing help bring production more in line with future market requirements as estimated by the Gordon commission on Canada's economic future.
With our rangeland potential almost fully exploited, the predicted large increase in the demand for beef would have to be met in our more adaptable cultivated areas, both east and west, through switching to grassland farming and, incidentally, putting more of our good land into effective preservation against the day when every available acre may have to be put under intensive cultivation in order to feed our own increasing population and high protein foods, such as beef, will be a luxury, as they are today in many parts of the world.
That the net income of competent farmers now on inadequate units could be increased by at least 50 per cent and their production made to conform more nearly to future market requirements with ample, long term, package deal credit made available to them was well established by a survey conducted by the Veterans' Land Act administration in 1958.
This survey covered a cross section of 25 per cent of Veterans' Land Act farm settlers in all provinces of Canada and was made for the purpose of assessing their future credit requirements. It was also so designed that it would show what effect the availability and use of adequate long term credit would have on their farm income and on their future production pattern, they having been previously exposed to at least some instruction having to do with modern farm organization and methods, particularly as applied to agriculture, through the services provided by federal farm credit advisers.
The results of this survey indicated that the most serious problems facing agriculture today may well stem from the lack of sufficient long term credit. It also seemed evident that ample, long term, package deal credit designed to assist competent young farmers in the setting up of family farm units of economic size, when granted in sufficient amounts to do the job for which it was intended, always enough but never too much, was probably the most effective and economical way in which the government could assist agriculture to attain parity of income with other industries, and this through the
Farm Credit Act
medium of reduced production costs from which the whole economy would benefit.
While this would be essentially a long term program, the assembly under a competent owner-operator of each and every new, economically sized family farm unit would bring agriculture one step nearer to the objective of parity income for its operators and production costs which would not only keep the home market but would make it possible to compete favourably in the export market as well.
The object of this legislation, as stated by the then minister of agriculture, is:
-to assist Canadian farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into economic family farm units, each of which will be of sufficient size or efficiency to produce the farm income necessary to pay all operating and maintenance costs; to provide a good livelihood for the owner-operator and his dependents; and to retire any required credit, with interest, within an appropriate term.
There are several reasons why this new credit program should be better than the old, the most important being that the corporation is operating under more comprehensive and forward looking credit legislation, with policy directed specifically toward the task of assisting the industry to reorganize itself into sound, economic family farm units.
Next in importance is the fact that the corporation has at its all-important field level a force of over 200 trained and experienced resident credit advisers who are now well deployed throughout the agricultural areas of the country. These have been drawn largely from trained and experienced V.L.A. farm credit advisers.
There is one area in the farm credit field that I feel merits careful consideration. In Manitoba, particularly, the size of the farm is not always a criterion for establishing an economic unit. I am advised by the farm credit corporation officials that it is the income potential rather than the unit size that provides a basis for their lending policy.
Where proper rotation, and careful husbandry is used, a loan to modernize equipment, or intensify the operation of the holding would be as satisfactory for increasing incomes as would a loan to enlarge the farm.
All farmers do not want to be big time operators. Many prefer to manage successfully on a small, but productive unit.
The fact that the farm credit corporation is seeking additional funds suggests that its credit facilities are being administered successfully under careful appraisal and supervision.
The continued use of these credit facilities by our farm people should have an important bearing on the income improvement of our rural communities, and the continuation of

Farm. Credit Act
the family farm, which is so essential to the economic well-being of the nation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext: Question.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
No. I should like to say a few words before the house passes this bill. The Farm Credit Act has been a matter of concern to me over the years and it has also been of concern to my constituents. The measure before us is designed to increase the amount which can be loaned under the act. It increases the amount of capital from $8 million to $12 million and as a result of the multiplication factor involved an additional $100 million will be made available for lending under the act.
This bill is a necessity because at the present time $165 million has been lent out and only $200 million can be lent, so before the end of the year the amount will have to be increased. We are now increasing it to $300 million. While discussing the total amount available for lending under the act I might point out that this government took action in 1958, under the old farm credit act, but $80 million was the limit of the amount which could be lent under it. In 1958 we increased the amount available under the farm credit act to $120 million but we saw the need for a still further increase and today the present bill will provide for $300 million to be lent out to farmers.
I may say that the act has worked reasonably well in most parts of Canada and perhaps in a large part of my own constituency but in my own constituency and in other parts of western Canada including northern and southern Alberta there are areas which are known as local improvement districts. These have certain special characteristics and the act as it now stands does not lend itself too readily to providing assistance in these particular areas. In my own constituency there are areas known as "special areas" somewhat similar in character to local improvement districts and here again the act as it now stands is not well adapted to the making of loans in those areas. I mentioned this in my maiden speech in 1958. Up until 1958, under the old act, there were no loans made in those particular areas. I may say there are about 3,000 farmers living in those areas and there is a demand for land and there is a change-over of land; this has been particularly the case in the last few years.
Again, the act may not be working too well in connection with the smaller farms as the minister himself suggested when he spoke this afternoon. I am thinking particularly of a case which was brought to my attention where a

farmer had been farming for the last ten or 15 years since the war on what we would call a small holding. He saw an opportunity to buy another quarter section recently adjoining his farmstead. He applied for a loan and his application was turned down because they thought his farm was not of an economic size. They said: if instead of $4,000 you are prepared to borrow $20,000 and buy an economic unit we will lend you the money, but we will not lend you $4,000. This particular farmer had been farming for 13 years He was a young man who had started farming in 1948 and who had acquired a lot of machinery, and perhaps a few debts with it, but he had been able to sustain himself and his family on a section of land. I think in this particular case he had a section and a quarter, and he had a lease on another half section. He wanted to buy another quarter section which he could have obtained for $4,000 but the corporation turned him down and said: you look around and try to find a large farm that is worth $20,000 and we will lend you the money.
These are some of the difficulties I have found in connection with the administration of this act. This particular farmer does not wish to move from his present farm. He wanted to add to it as adjacent land became available. Had he bought the other quarter section he might not have been through adding to it. He might have continued to add to it from year to year and maybe at the end of five or six years he would have built his loan up to $20,000. I think the corporation should have taken into consideration the fact that this particular farmer had been existing on his farm site. He wanted to add to his land as property became available. It is true he might not have had what some persons would consider to be an economic unit but we all know the difficulty of defining an economic unit. Acreage certainly enters into it, but acreage is not the only factor. It depends on how intensively the acreage is farmed. So I hope the men in charge of the administration of this act will pay particular attention to these things. I note that other hon. members who have spoken in connection with this measure tonight have encountered situations where this idea of what constitutes an economic unit in a given area sometimes varies to a large extent according to the peculiarities of a given locality. I certainly think there is a great deal of variation in what constitutes an economic unit and how it should be appraised in any particular area.
The particular areas I mentioned a while ago, the "special areas", are generally considered by some to be ranching country. But

there are lots of good farming spots in central Alberta-lots of places where the farmer can sustain himself and his family on a section and a half or two sections of land. In other areas he may need closer to ten sections. So I hope the authorities will be more ready to lend a small sum of money rather than trying to encourage young farmers to borrow the largest amounts in order to buy well established farms. It is today very difficult to find a well established farm or what most individuals would consider to be an economic unit, for less than $20,000. I think the farmer who wishes to enlarge, develop or perhaps intensify his farm operations, should surely be able to do so with credit obtained under this particular measure.
The minister made brief reference to the suggestion of accepting leased land as security for loans made under this act. I should like to enlarge upon that subject.
In my particular area the farmers have had a great deal of difficulty in using leased land as security for loans under the act. I realize that authorities have suggested that a loan on this basis could qualify under part III of the act as it now stands. However, I should like to point out that under part III of the act a potential borrower cannot purchase land in respect to which he is a tenant farmer. I can see no reason why the farm credit corporation should not accept a lease in its name, allowing a farmer to borrow money in order to develop that land until he has paid the loan, at which time the lease would then revert to his own name.
In a great many areas of southwestern Saskatchewan, southeastern Alberta, and even the southwestern portion of Alberta along the foothills, a great deal of leased land is used for agricultural purposes. In my particular area leases change hands at the rate of $3 to $6 per acre. That is not a lot of money, and certainly a farmer would not have to borrow much money under this act to buy land of that type at that price, and would be in a position to repay the loan within a relatively short period of time. If the farmer had enough livestock he could use that as security for a loan under the farm credit corporation measure along with his leased land, put in the name of the corporation, and would then find himself in a position to pay back the loan within a few years, at which time the lease would revert to his own name. I understand that the Veterans' Land Act administration has worked closely with the farm credit corporation administration. I should like to point out to the minister that I am aware of certain cases where the Veterans' Land Act administration has accepted leases in its name as
Farm Credit Act
security for loans. I suggest this same practice could be followed by the administration of this act.
There has been some mention made during the debate this afternoon of the subsidization provided under this act. The idea has been expressed that there might be a continued subsidization in this regard. I take strong exception to those suggestions, because last year was the first year for a long period of time that the farm credit corporation, or the farm loans act, lost money.
The government is now in a position to borrow money from the Bank of Canada, if I read the figures correctly, at an interest rate of between 3.3 per cent and 4 per cent. I say that because of articles appearing in various newspapers recently. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) frowning at me. Perhaps the interest rate is 3.30 per cent.
In any event the interest rate is between 3 per cent and 4 per cent. In view of that fact, I see no reason why the government cannot borrow money at that interest rate, and make loans under this act to farmers because, as the minister stated last night, the operation cost amounted to only .8 per cent. Under this act, borrowers must pay 5 per cent interest, so that even if the government had to pay 4 per cent on its borrowings, it could do so and make these loans at a profit.
For the reasons I have set out, I cannot understand why this measure is considered to be a subsidization at all.
Some hon. members might feel that this particular measure does not concern the farmers in my area. I should like to point out that under section 27 of the act a loan can be made to cover a complete farming operation, using the farmers chattels as security, only if the loan is made under part III of the act. In addition, there are further stipulations which must be met. The first important stipulation is that a farmer cannot borrow, under part III of the act, at the same time as he has a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. As an example of the difficulty involved here I should cite the case of a farmer farming an area, who desires to purchase additional land through a loan under part III of the act. Having done so, he would be prohibited from borrowing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in order to purchase new or additional machinery to farm his land. While there may be a few isolated cases where an individual has used the same piece of machinery as security for two different loans, I see no difficulty in that regard under the application of part III, because when a young farmer makes application to the bank for a loan under the Farm

Farm Credit Act
Improvement Loans Act, the banker makes absolutely sure that the machinery used as security is clear of encumbrances.
I suggest the individuals who will take advantage of the loans available under this new legislation will be young fanners with a desire to purchase their father's holdings, and will be required to borrow close to the maximum amount. If those individuals accept supervision, they would make loans under part III of this act. Having done so they would not then be able to borrow money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act to purchase additional machinery, until such time as the original loan was reduced to less than $20,000. I can foresee complications arising because of the application of part III, and I do not understand the reason for its inclusion in the act.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to touch upon one other subject before I conclude, having to do with the appraisal fee. Most hon. members are perhaps aware that the appraisal fee is now set at 2 per cent of the amount of the loan, or $100, whichever is the lesser. I feel it is unnecessary to increase this appraisal fee from $10 to $100. I suggest this has caused a great deal of concern and hardship to those farmers who must pay the $100 appraisal fee in addition to the cost of finding out whether the title to the land is clear. I suggest that the total cost to the farmer, when making application for a loan under this measure, including the appraisal fee, might well be $200. That fact in itself perhaps would not be such a great problem if there was any assurance to the farmer that, having paid out that money, his application would be approved. In some instances farmers are apt to have an appraisal made, pay $100 and be turned down after the appraisal is made. Although the farmer is turned down, he still has to pay the $100. This is a hardship on a particular farmer who is thus prevented from enlarging his present holdings, as was the case in the instance I mentioned earlier this evening.
I should like to see some changes made in this regulation, perhaps not at this session but in the year to come, and the appraisal fee be reduced to $10 as it was formerly. If the applicant is turned down, or if the appraisal is not made, the fee should be refunded. This is a small point but I thought I should mention it because I know some of the difficulties that some farmers have had in my constituency in trying to get loans under this particular act. I might say that only the one area in my constituency has had this trouble. Farmers in this area have been turned down on a number of occasions because, as I said, they did not want to borrow too much money. They just wanted to

borrow a little to add to their present holdings. Sometimes an appraiser would come into the drier part of Alberta and not recommend the loan. The country is dry, so much so that some people have claimed the gophers have moved out. Actually it is not that bad. Farmers in that particular area are as good security risks as farmers in any other part of the province. They have proved this over the years.
I would strongly recommend that an appraiser be placed in this particular area because of the number of applicants that have been turned down. An appraiser coming from some of the more fertile parts of Alberta, the parts fortunate enough to receive a great deal of rain, drives into this dry country and says, "Oh my gosh, I would not lend a plugged nickel in this country", and drives out again. A farmer trying to borrow some money is put in the position where his case is not properly viewed in the light that perhaps he would hope it would be, and he is turned down almost automatically because he is living in that particular area.

I know that the president of the corporation has recently appointed Mr. Carr, chief land appraiser from Ottawa, to make a study of the whole lease problem in western Canada. I refer to the land that is leased in the area between the lakes in Manitoba and in southwestern Saskatchewan, in Alberta and in British Columbia. This land is leased by farmers and ranchers who are in the agricultural industry. The leased land changes hand from time to time, sometimes at high prices and sometimes at rather low prices. Certainly, those farmers should have the opportunity to adjust the size of their units, to make them more economic and to borrow money under this particular act. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for bearing with me for a moment while I got this particular thought across.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see this change and I should like to say a few words on the bill.
So far as I can ascertain, the remarks that have been made so far have all been in favour of this legislation. The reason that we are in favour of the increase in the amount of money is that there has been a new director appointed under the Farm Credit Act. We should be appreciative of the job he has been able to do in such a short time. The fact that we need more money under the Farm Credit Act now is an indication that the act is working for the first time in a long period of time.
It has always seemed to me that borrowing money from the Canadian farm loan board was a little bit like trying to borrow money from the treasury board or going to the Minister of Finance and asking him for a loan. The administrators of the act were not the least bit interested in lending money. There were certain requirements. If you fitted into that particular limited pattern then you got the money. Mr. Rutherford, the former director of the Veterans' Land Act did have experience. His officials had the approach of wanting to lend money that was going to be advantageous to the farmers. You did not lend the money whether the person needed it or not. Previously it depended on whether the farmer fitted into a little slot. It did not depend necessarily on whether it was advantageous to the farmer; he got the money if he met certain requirements. Now it seems no matter whether the money is asked for under
Farm Credit Act
supervision or not there is continuously a certain amount of supervision. It seems to me this is the only way that money being lent to farmers is going to be advantageously used by those farmers. Although farmers may not readily admit it, they need assistance in ascertaining how much help they need. The hon. member who just took his seat spoke of areas of 10,000 acres. This certainly does not apply in my area.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext: If the hon. member is referring to my remarks, I said 10 sections or 2 sections.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
I am sorry if I misquoted the hon. member. It would not make any difference. Ten sections are still a great deal more than the area on which farmers in my constituency are going to be borrowing money, if it is a very large amount of land. It has been a factor. I presume the hon. member was referring to the need for larger farms to make up an economic unit. There has been a tendency for farmers to borrow money on an uneconomical unit. Obviously his borrowing of that money was not going to enable him to better his position very much.
One of the things to the credit of the Veterans' Land Act administration was the ability of the officials to supervise and the advice they gave. This practice is now being applied generally to Canadian farm loans and it means that the farmer is receiving some assistance and technical advice that he did not have the opportunity to obtain before. The advice is being given in such a manner that the farmer will accept it because it is not completely dependent upon the loan or the conditions of the loan. In my area, for example, farmers have been advised that if they plant certain crops the market is such and such and if they plant something else their chances of obtaining a better price per acre of produce will be much more readily realized. In some instances technical advice has been given in relation to the operation of the farm.
It seems to me that the technical assistance being given in this way by the officials is a great advantage over the system that obtained before. The Farm Credit Act agents are going to the farms and talking to the farmer and his wife. They are assessing the situation themselves and in my opinion this is doing a great deal to enable the farmer to obtain an advantageous loan, one which he is going to be able to repay and which it is to his advantage to obtain.
The fact that the government is asking for an increase in the amount of money available for loans is an indication that this credit system is an advantageous one. With its experience under this act, I believe that the

Farm Credit Act
government is going to give consideration to increasing the supervision under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. There is a similarity between the two acts. As a previous speaker mentioned, they are interrelated to some extent and they certainly work advantageously in combination.
Having in mind the inquiry into farm machinery that is now under way, I believe it is increasingly advantageous for the farmer to have impartial advice with relation to the purchase of new machinery because occasionally we find that rather than the farmer wanting to buy, the machinery companies are persuading him to buy. A little advice may help to prevent some farmers from trying to keep up with the Jones'. It seems to me that this act is a credit to the government. We are very pleased with the way it has been operating and with the fact that more money is necessary. We are also pleased that the bill has been introduced and will be passed before the budget is brought down because it might be more difficult at that time.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house long. At the resolution stage of this measure last night one point was raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). He asked why it was that the resolution made no reference to the provisions in the measure in relation to the assignment of debts.
